ai-c1-t01.title: Definition of an AI
ai-c1-t01.definition: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science that builds machines/software able to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence.
ai-c1-t01.simpleExplanation: AI ka matlab hai computer ko aisa banana ki wo sirf instructions follow na kare, balki seekhe, reason kare, decide kare aur problems solve kare. Ek normal program fixed steps chalata hai; AI program situation ke hisaab se behave karta hai.
ai-c1-t01.realLifeAnalogy: A normal calculator is like a student who only follows the formula you give. An AI system is like a student who looks at past questions, figures out the pattern and solves a new question on his own.
ai-c1-t01.example: Spam filter: input = email text; the system checks word patterns/sender history and outputs 'spam' or 'not spam'. Nobody wrote a rule for every possible spam mail — it generalises. Russell & Norvig's four views: (1) thinking humanly – cognitive modelling, (2) thinking rationally – laws of thought/logic, (3) acting humanly – Turing Test, (4) acting rationally – rational agent.
keyPoints: John McCarthy coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' (1955–56).
Four views: thinking/acting humanly, thinking/acting rationally.
Turing Test (1950): machine passes if a human interrogator cannot tell it from a human.
Acting rationally (rational agent) is the most widely used modern view.
AI = perception + reasoning + learning + action.
Narrow (weak) AI does specific tasks; General (strong) AI would match human ability across tasks.
mustKnow: McCarthy's definition: the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.
Turing Test idea and its limitation (tests behaviour, not understanding).
ifYouKnow: List the four approaches to AI.
Distinguish weak AI from strong AI.
Answer 'Is a chess program intelligent?' in a viva.
commonMistakes: Thinking AI = only machine learning. ML is one part of AI, not all of it.
Believing the Turing Test checks whether a machine really 'understands' — it only checks indistinguishable behaviour.
Confusing 'acting rationally' with 'acting like a human' — a rational agent may behave very un-humanly.

examQuestions.question: Define Artificial Intelligence.
examQuestions.answer: The science and engineering of making intelligent machines, especially intelligent programs, that can perceive, reason, learn and act to achieve goals.

examQuestions.question: Explain the four approaches to AI.
examQuestions.answer: Acting humanly (Turing Test), thinking humanly (cognitive science), thinking rationally (logic/laws of thought), acting rationally (rational agent that does the best action for its goal).

examQuestions.question: Explain the Turing Test.
examQuestions.answer: Proposed by Alan Turing (1950). A human judge chats with a hidden human and a hidden machine; if the judge cannot reliably tell which is the machine, the machine passes. Example: a chatbot answering open questions like a person.

examQuestions.question: Difference between weak and strong AI?
examQuestions.answer: Weak AI is built for a specific task (e.g. chess, spam filter). Strong AI would have human-level general intelligence across any task; it does not exist yet.

knowledgeCheck.question: Who coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence'?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: McCarthy named the field for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

knowledgeCheck.question: The Turing Test measures whether a machine truly understands language.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It only tests whether behaviour is indistinguishable from a human.

knowledgeCheck.question: Name the four approaches to AI.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Thinking humanly, thinking rationally, acting humanly, acting rationally.

knowledgeCheck.question: Weak AI vs Strong AI — one difference.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Weak AI performs a specific task; strong AI would have general human-level intelligence.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: All existing systems are weak/narrow AI.

knowledgeCheck.question: A voice assistant answers questions but cannot drive a car. Which AI type is it?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It is limited to a specific domain.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which approach does a modern 'rational agent' follow?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It chooses the action expected to best achieve its goal.

ai-c1-t01.quickRevision: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science that builds machines/software able to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence. Remember: McCarthy's definition: the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.

ai-c1-t02.title: Major Areas of Artificial Intelligence
ai-c1-t02.definition: The major areas of AI are the main sub-fields that attack different parts of intelligence, such as learning, language, vision, reasoning and robotics.
ai-c1-t02.simpleExplanation: AI ek bada umbrella hai. Neeche alag-alag fields hain: koi machine ko seekhna sikhata hai (ML), koi language samajhna (NLP), koi dekhna (Vision), koi chalna/kaam karna (Robotics).
ai-c1-t02.realLifeAnalogy: AI is like a hospital: it has different departments (heart, eye, brain). Each AI area is a department focused on one ability.
ai-c1-t02.example: Self-driving car uses many areas together: computer vision (see lanes), ML (learn driving), planning (route), robotics/control (steer), and sensors fusion.
keyPoints: Machine Learning – learns patterns from data.
Natural Language Processing – understands/generates human language.
Computer Vision – interprets images/video.
Robotics – perception + action in the physical world.
Expert Systems – capture a human expert's knowledge in rules.
Knowledge Representation & Reasoning – store facts and infer new ones.
Speech recognition, Game playing, Planning, Fuzzy logic, Neural networks.
mustKnow: List at least 6 areas with one-line use each.
Expert systems = knowledge base + inference engine.
Neural networks/Deep learning are a part of ML.
ifYouKnow: Name the major areas of AI.
Give one application of each area.
Say which area a given system (e.g. Siri, Tesla Autopilot) belongs to.
Explain how areas combine in one product.
commonMistakes: Treating ML, deep learning and AI as the same thing (AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning).
Thinking robotics = AI; robots without learning/reasoning are just machines.

examQuestions.question: Explain major areas of AI with examples.
examQuestions.answer: ML (recommendations), NLP (translation), Vision (face unlock), Robotics (warehouse robots), Expert systems (medical diagnosis), Speech (voice assistants), Game playing (chess engines), Planning (route/logistics).

examQuestions.question: Relation between AI, ML and Deep Learning?
examQuestions.answer: AI is the broad goal; ML is a way to achieve it by learning from data; deep learning is ML using multi-layer neural networks.

examQuestions.question: Which AI area does Google Translate belong to?
examQuestions.answer: Natural Language Processing (using ML/neural networks).

knowledgeCheck.question: Face-unlock on a phone mainly uses:
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning.
What are the two main parts of an expert system?
A chatbot reads a customer's complaint and replies. Which area?
NLP vs Speech recognition.
knowledgeCheck.answer: NLP understands/generates language (text); speech recognition converts spoken audio into text.

ai-c1-t02.quickRevision: The major areas of AI are the main sub-fields that attack different parts of intelligence, such as learning, language, vision, reasoning and robotics. Remember: List at least 6 areas with one-line use each.

ai-c1-t03.title: AI Techniques
ai-c1-t03.definition: An AI technique is a method that exploits knowledge, represented so it can be generalised and modified, to solve hard problems by narrowing the search.
ai-c1-t03.simpleExplanation: Hard problems me possibilities bahut hoti hain. AI technique ka kaam hai: knowledge use karke sahi raste ko jaldi dhundna, har possibility check kiye bina.
ai-c1-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Finding a shop in a big mall: brute force means visiting every shop; an AI technique is using the directory board (knowledge) and heading straight to the right floor.
ai-c1-t03.example: Tic-tac-toe: Program 1 stores a lookup table of all board positions (huge, rigid). Program 2 uses a magic-square trick (smaller). Program 3 searches the game tree with look-ahead (minimax) — it generalises and is easy to extend. Each step uses more knowledge/structure.
keyPoints: Rich & Knight: AI techniques use knowledge, search and abstraction.
Search – systematically explore possible states for a goal.
Use of knowledge – rules/heuristics that guide the search.
Abstraction – ignore unimportant details, focus on essentials.
Good knowledge representation: captures generalisations, is understandable, easy to modify, usable even if not fully accurate, and reduces the search space.
mustKnow: Three core techniques: search, use of knowledge, abstraction.
Tic-tac-toe example showing improvement in techniques.
ifYouKnow: Explain the tic-tac-toe programs at a high level.
commonMistakes: Thinking AI technique = a particular algorithm; it is a general approach (search + knowledge + abstraction).
Believing more knowledge always means faster — wrong or huge knowledge can itself slow reasoning.

examQuestions.question: What is an AI technique? Name its components.
examQuestions.answer: A method that uses knowledge to solve complex problems. Components: search, use of knowledge, abstraction.

examQuestions.question: Explain AI technique using tic-tac-toe.
examQuestions.answer: Table lookup → magic square → minimax with look-ahead; each version uses knowledge more generally and is easier to extend.

examQuestions.question: What is abstraction in AI?
examQuestions.answer: Separating important features from unimportant details so the problem becomes smaller and manageable.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is NOT a core AI technique?
Abstraction means adding more details to the problem.
Why is knowledge important in AI?
knowledgeCheck.answer: It guides the search and narrows the number of possibilities.

knowledgeCheck.question: A route planner ignores road colour and only considers distance/traffic. Which technique?
Tic-tac-toe lookup table needs 3^9 entries approx. Why is that a weak technique?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Too much memory, no generalisation, hard to modify.

ai-c1-t03.quickRevision: An AI technique is a method that exploits knowledge, represented so it can be generalised and modified, to solve hard problems by narrowing the search. Remember: Three core techniques: search, use of knowledge, abstraction.

ai-c1-t04.title: History of AI
ai-c1-t04.definition: The history of AI is the timeline of the field from early ideas of machine intelligence (1940s) to today's deep learning and large language models.
ai-c1-t04.simpleExplanation: AI achanak nahi aaya. Pehle bade sapne aaye, phir funding gayi (AI winters), phir data aur powerful GPUs ke saath deep learning se boom aaya.
ai-c1-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Like a cricket team's journey: early enthusiasm, long losing streaks, then a comeback with better training (data and hardware).
ai-c1-t04.example: Timeline: 1943 McCulloch–Pitts neuron → 1950 Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' → 1956 Dartmouth Conference (term 'AI'), Logic Theorist → 1966 ELIZA → 1970s first AI winter → 1980s expert systems (XCON) → late-80s second winter → 1997 Deep Blue beats Kasparov → 2011 Watson wins Jeopardy! → 2012 deep learning (AlexNet) → 2016 AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol → 2017 Transformer → 2020s large language models.
keyPoints: 1950: Turing proposes the Turing Test.
1956: Dartmouth Conference – birth of AI as a field.
1966: ELIZA, an early chatbot.
AI winters: periods of reduced funding after unmet promises (1970s, late 1980s).
1980s: expert systems boom.
1997: Deep Blue defeats world chess champion.
2012 onward: deep learning revolution (big data + GPUs).
mustKnow: Two AI winters and why they happened.
ifYouKnow: Explain what an AI winter is.
commonMistakes: Saying AI began with ChatGPT — the field started in the 1950s.
Mixing up Deep Blue (chess, 1997) and AlphaGo (Go, 2016).

examQuestions.question: Write a short note on history of AI.
examQuestions.answer: Include 1943 neuron model, 1950 Turing test, 1956 Dartmouth, 1960s early programs, 1970s winter, 1980s expert systems, 1997 Deep Blue, 2012 deep learning, 2016 AlphaGo, 2020s LLMs.

examQuestions.question: What is an AI winter?
examQuestions.answer: A period of reduced funding and interest in AI after over-promised results failed.

examQuestions.question: Which event is considered the birth of AI?
examQuestions.answer: The 1956 Dartmouth Conference.

knowledgeCheck.question: The term 'AI' was coined at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
Give one reason for the AI winters.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Over-promised results and limited computing power/data led to funding cuts.

knowledgeCheck.question: Deep Blue vs AlphaGo.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Deep Blue (1997) played chess using brute-force search + evaluation; AlphaGo (2016) played Go using deep neural networks and reinforcement learning.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Go has a much larger search space.

ai-c1-t04.quickRevision: The history of AI is the timeline of the field from early ideas of machine intelligence (1940s) to today's deep learning and large language models. Remember: Dartmouth 1956 and McCarthy.

ai-c1-t05.title: AI Problems
ai-c1-t05.definition: AI problems are tasks that humans find easy or require expertise but are hard for computers, grouped into mundane, formal and expert tasks.
ai-c1-t05.simpleExplanation: Kuch kaam insaan ke liye bahut easy hain (dekhna, bolna) par computer ke liye mushkil. Kuch kaam sirf experts karte hain. Ye sab AI problems hain.
ai-c1-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A toddler recognises mom's face instantly but cannot do calculus; a computer multiplies huge numbers instantly but struggles to recognise a face. AI works on bridging that gap.
ai-c1-t05.example: Medical diagnosis (expert task): input symptoms and test results; the system applies rules/probabilities to suggest a likely disease, as MYCIN did for bacterial infections.
keyPoints: Mundane tasks: perception (vision, speech), natural language, commonsense reasoning, robot control.
Formal tasks: games (chess), mathematics (geometry, logic, integral calculus), theorem proving.
Expert tasks: engineering design, scientific analysis, medical diagnosis, financial analysis.
Mundane tasks are easy for humans but hard for AI; expert tasks need domain knowledge.
mustKnow: Why mundane tasks are hard: huge knowledge, ambiguity, noise.
ifYouKnow: Give two examples of each category.
Explain why vision is harder than chess.
commonMistakes: Assuming chess is the hardest AI problem; everyday perception is harder.
Mixing 'formal' tasks with 'expert' tasks.

examQuestions.question: Explain categories of AI problems.
examQuestions.answer: Mundane (perception, NLP, commonsense), formal (games, theorem proving, maths), expert (diagnosis, design, analysis) with examples.

examQuestions.question: Is speech recognition a mundane or expert task?
examQuestions.answer: Mundane (perception).

knowledgeCheck.question: Playing chess is a formal task.
A system proves geometry theorems. Which category?
Formal vs expert tasks.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Formal tasks have clear rules (games/maths); expert tasks need specialised domain knowledge (diagnosis/design).

ai-c1-t05.quickRevision: AI problems are tasks that humans find easy or require expertise but are hard for computers, grouped into mundane, formal and expert tasks. Remember: Three categories and examples (Rich & Knight).

ai-c1-t06.title: Production Systems
ai-c1-t06.definition: A production system is an AI model made of a set of IF-THEN rules, a working memory (database), and a control strategy that chooses which rule to apply.
ai-c1-t06.simpleExplanation: Production system me problem ko rules se solve karte hain: 'agar ye condition hai to ye action lo'. Database current state rakhta hai aur control strategy decide karti hai kaunsa rule pehle chalna hai.
ai-c1-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Think of a board game rulebook: the board is the current state, the rules say what moves are allowed, and the player (control strategy) picks one of the legal moves.
ai-c1-t06.example: Water jug (4L and 3L, goal: exactly 2L in the 4L jug). State (x,y). Rules e.g. (x,y), x<4 → (4,y); (x,y), y>0 → (x,0). Solution: (0,0)→(0,3)→(3,0)→(3,3)→(4,2)→(0,2)→(2,0). Goal reached.
keyPoints: Components: set of production rules, global database (working memory), control strategy, rule applier.
Rule form: condition → action.
Control strategy resolves conflicts when many rules match.
Types: monotonic, non-monotonic, commutative, partially commutative.
Used in expert systems, planning and games.
Control strategy must cause motion and be systematic.
mustKnow: Four components of a production system.
Water jug rules and a solution path.
ifYouKnow: Write rules for the water jug problem.
commonMistakes: Thinking rules are applied in program order — the control strategy decides.
Ignoring that applying a rule changes the database state.
Confusing production rules with programming IF-ELSE; they are separate from control flow.

examQuestions.question: Define production system and its components.
examQuestions.answer: Set of rules + working memory + control strategy (+ rule applier). Rules have condition-action form.

examQuestions.question: Solve the 4L/3L water jug problem to get 2L.
Monotonic vs non-monotonic production system.
examQuestions.answer: In a monotonic system applying a rule never prevents another applicable rule from being applied later; in non-monotonic it can.

examQuestions.question: What is conflict resolution?
examQuestions.answer: Choosing one rule when several rules' conditions match the current state.

knowledgeCheck.question: A production rule has the form:
The control strategy decides which applicable rule is fired.
Name the components of a production system.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Production rules, working memory/database, control strategy.

knowledgeCheck.question: From (3,0) in the water jug problem, fill the 3L jug. New state?
Commutative vs non-commutative systems.
knowledgeCheck.answer: In a commutative system the order of applicable rules does not matter to reach the goal; otherwise order matters.

ai-c1-t06.quickRevision: A production system is an AI model made of a set of IF-THEN rules, a working memory (database), and a control strategy that chooses which rule to apply. Remember: Four components of a production system.

ai-c1-t07.title: Problem Characteristics
ai-c1-t07.definition: Problem characteristics are properties of a problem (decomposable, ignorable/recoverable, predictable, any-path/best-path, etc.) that decide which AI method suits it.
ai-c1-t07.simpleExplanation: Har problem ek jaisa nahi hota. Pehle problem ko analyse karte hain: kya chhote parts me tod sakte hain? galti undo ho sakti hai? best solution chahiye ya koi bhi? Phir sahi technique chunte hain.
ai-c1-t07.realLifeAnalogy: Before choosing a vehicle you ask: how far, how many people, how much luggage? Problem characteristics are those questions before choosing the algorithm.
ai-c1-t07.example: Chess: not decomposable, irrecoverable (moves can't be undone), uncertain (opponent), best-path needed. 8-puzzle: recoverable (can undo moves), certain outcome. Theorem proving: ignorable (a useless step can be ignored).
keyPoints: Decomposable? Can it be split into independent sub-problems (symbolic integration)?
Ignorable / recoverable / irrecoverable steps (theorem proving / 8-puzzle / chess).
Predictable universe? certain-outcome vs uncertain-outcome.
Any-path vs best-path solution (water jug vs travelling salesman).
Solution is a state or a path?
Role of knowledge; need for human interaction.
ifYouKnow: Classify chess, 8-puzzle and TSP on them.
Choose suitable technique for a problem.
commonMistakes: Mixing recoverable and ignorable: ignorable steps can be skipped; recoverable steps can be undone.
Saying all search problems need the best path — many need any path.

examQuestions.question: Explain problem characteristics with examples.
examQuestions.answer: Decomposable, ignorable/recoverable/irrecoverable, predictable, any-path/best-path, state vs path solution, role of knowledge; give chess/8-puzzle/TSP examples.

examQuestions.question: Ignorable vs recoverable vs irrecoverable.
examQuestions.answer: Ignorable: step can be ignored (theorem proving); recoverable: step can be undone (8-puzzle); irrecoverable: cannot be undone (chess).

knowledgeCheck.question: Travelling salesman is a best-path problem.
What does decomposable mean?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The problem can be split into independent smaller sub-problems.

knowledgeCheck.question: Water jug: any sequence reaching 2L is fine. Which type?
Any-path vs best-path.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Any-path accepts the first solution; best-path searches for an optimal solution.

ai-c1-t07.quickRevision: Problem characteristics are properties of a problem (decomposable, ignorable/recoverable, predictable, any-path/best-path, etc.) that decide which AI method suits it. Remember: Rich & Knight's characteristics list.

ai-c1-t08.title: Intelligent Agents
ai-c1-t08.definition: An intelligent agent is an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators to achieve its goals.
ai-c1-t08.simpleExplanation: Agent ek system hai jo environment ko dekhta hai (sensors se) aur action leta hai (actuators se). Rational agent wo hai jo best expected result ke liye sahi action chunta hai.
ai-c1-t08.realLifeAnalogy: A robot vacuum: sensors detect dirt/walls, wheels and brush are actuators, and its goal is a clean floor.
ai-c1-t08.example: Vacuum world: percepts = [location, dirty/clean]; actions = Left, Right, Suck. Rule: if dirty → Suck, else move. PEAS: Performance = clean squares over time; Environment = two rooms; Actuators = wheels, suction; Sensors = dirt sensor, location sensor.
keyPoints: Agent = anything that perceives (sensors) and acts (actuators).
Agent function maps percept sequence → action.
Rational agent maximises expected performance measure.
PEAS: Performance, Environment, Actuators, Sensors.
Environment properties: fully/partially observable, deterministic/stochastic, episodic/sequential, static/dynamic, discrete/continuous, single/multi-agent.
mustKnow: Rationality depends on performance measure, prior knowledge, actions, percept sequence.
ifYouKnow: Define an agent and rational agent.
Write PEAS for taxi / vacuum / chess.
commonMistakes: Rational ≠ omniscient: it maximises expected, not actual, success.
Confusing agent function (abstract mapping) with agent program (implementation).

examQuestions.question: What is an intelligent agent? What is a rational agent?
examQuestions.answer: Agent perceives via sensors and acts via actuators; rational agent selects actions expected to maximise its performance measure.

examQuestions.question: Write PEAS for an automated taxi.
examQuestions.answer: P: safe, fast, legal, comfortable trips; E: roads, traffic, pedestrians; A: steering, accelerator, brake, horn; S: cameras, GPS, speedometer, sensors.

examQuestions.question: Is a rational agent always successful?
examQuestions.answer: No, it is only expected to do the best given its knowledge.

knowledgeCheck.question: A rational agent is always omniscient.
What is an actuator?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A component through which the agent acts on the environment (e.g. wheels).

knowledgeCheck.question: Chess vs poker: which is fully observable?
Deterministic vs stochastic environment.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Deterministic: next state fully determined by current state and action; stochastic: has randomness/uncertainty.

ai-c1-t08.quickRevision: An intelligent agent is an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators to achieve its goals. Remember: Definition + PEAS.

ai-c1-t09.title: Agent Architecture
ai-c1-t09.definition: Agent architecture is the computing platform with sensors and actuators on which the agent program runs; agent = architecture + program.
ai-c1-t09.simpleExplanation: Agent ka structure batata hai ki wo percept se action tak kaise pahunchta hai. Simple reflex se leke learning agent tak 5 types hote hain, har ek zyada smart.
ai-c1-t09.realLifeAnalogy: Simple reflex is like pulling your hand from a hot pan; goal-based is planning a route; utility-based is choosing the route that is quickest and safest; learning agent improves with every trip.
ai-c1-t09.example: Thermostat = simple reflex (if temp>25 → cooling on). Self-driving car = utility-based (balances speed, safety, comfort). Spam filter that improves from user feedback = learning agent.
keyPoints: Agent = architecture + agent program.
Simple reflex agent: condition–action rules on current percept only.
Model-based reflex: keeps internal state of the world.
Goal-based: chooses actions to reach a goal (uses search/planning).
Utility-based: maximises a utility (degree of happiness) when many ways reach the goal.
Learning agent: learning element, critic, performance element, problem generator.
mustKnow: Five agent types and their order.
Table of when each type is used.
ifYouKnow: Choose agent type for a scenario.
commonMistakes: Thinking simple reflex agents use memory; they use only the current percept.
Confusing goal-based (goal reached or not) with utility-based (how good the outcome is).

examQuestions.question: Explain types of agents with diagrams.
examQuestions.answer: Simple reflex, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based, learning; each adds state, goals, utility or learning.

examQuestions.question: Goal-based vs utility-based agent.
examQuestions.answer: Goal-based: only goal achieved or not; utility-based: compares outcomes using a utility function.

examQuestions.question: Which agent has a critic?
examQuestions.answer: Learning agent.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which agent uses only the current percept?
What does the critic do in a learning agent?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Gives feedback on how well the agent is doing against a performance standard.

knowledgeCheck.question: A thermostat turns AC on above 25°C. Agent type?
Model-based vs simple reflex.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Model-based maintains internal state of the unseen world; simple reflex does not.

ai-c1-t09.quickRevision: Agent architecture is the computing platform with sensors and actuators on which the agent program runs; agent = architecture + program. Remember: Five agent types and their order.

ai-c1-t10.title: AI Application (E-Commerce & Medicine)
ai-c1-t10.definition: AI applications in e-commerce and medicine apply AI techniques to personalise shopping, automate business tasks, and support diagnosis and treatment.
ai-c1-t10.simpleExplanation: E-commerce me AI aapko wo products dikhata hai jo aap khareedna chahoge. Medicine me AI scans aur data dekhkar doctors ko disease pehchanne me help karta hai.
ai-c1-t10.realLifeAnalogy: In e-commerce AI is a smart shopkeeper who remembers your taste; in medicine it is a tireless assistant who has read millions of case files.
ai-c1-t10.example: E-commerce: Amazon recommends products using collaborative filtering (people with similar purchases). Medicine: a deep-learning model reads chest X-rays and flags possible pneumonia for the radiologist to confirm.
keyPoints: E-commerce: recommendation engines, chatbots, dynamic pricing, fraud detection, demand forecasting, visual search.
Medicine: medical imaging analysis, diagnosis support, drug discovery, robotic surgery, patient monitoring, personalised treatment.
Benefits: speed, personalisation, accuracy.
Concerns: privacy, bias, explainability, need for human oversight.
mustKnow: Two applications per domain with technique used.
ifYouKnow: State one risk in medical AI.
commonMistakes: Saying AI replaces doctors — it supports them.
Believing recommendations are random; they use user behaviour data.

examQuestions.question: Explain applications of AI in e-commerce and medicine.
examQuestions.answer: E-commerce: recommendations, chatbots, pricing, fraud detection. Medicine: imaging diagnosis, drug discovery, surgery robots, monitoring.

examQuestions.question: How does a recommendation engine work?
examQuestions.answer: It finds patterns in browsing/purchase history of similar users or products and suggests items likely to be bought.

knowledgeCheck.question: Fraud detection in online payments uses:
AI in medicine is used only for surgery.
Name one ethical concern in medical AI.
An app shows 'customers also bought'. Technique?
Which medical expert system diagnosed bacterial infections?

ai-c1-t10.quickRevision: AI applications in e-commerce and medicine apply AI techniques to personalise shopping, automate business tasks, and support diagnosis and treatment. Remember: Two applications per domain with technique used.

ai-c1-t11.title: AI Representation
ai-c1-t11.definition: AI representation is the way facts about the world are encoded in a form a program can store and reason with.
ai-c1-t11.simpleExplanation: Computer English nahi samajhta. Isliye real-world facts ko ek internal form (logic, rules, frames) me convert karte hain. Reasoning internal form pe hoti hai, phir answer wapas English me.
ai-c1-t11.realLifeAnalogy: Like a map: the real city is too big to carry, so you use a map (representation) that keeps what you need for finding routes.
ai-c1-t11.example: Fact: 'Marcus is a man.' Representation in logic: man(Marcus). Fact: 'All men are mortal': ∀x man(x) → mortal(x). Reasoning gives mortal(Marcus), which is mapped back to English.
keyPoints: Facts ↔ internal representation via forward and backward mapping.
Reasoning operates on the internal representation.
Common forms: logic, semantic nets, frames, production rules.
Representation affects how easy or hard the reasoning is.
A representation must keep important information and ignore the rest.
mustKnow: Mapping diagram: Facts → Representation → Reasoning → Representation → Facts.
ifYouKnow: Convert a simple sentence to logic.
commonMistakes: Thinking representation = data structure only; it also needs operations for inference.
Assuming one representation fits all problems.

examQuestions.question: What is knowledge representation? Why needed?
examQuestions.answer: Encoding facts in a computer-usable form so programs can store, reason and answer; needed because machines cannot work directly with natural language.

examQuestions.question: Show mapping between facts and representation.
examQuestions.answer: English fact → forward mapping → logic sentence → inference → new sentence → backward mapping → English.

knowledgeCheck.question: Reasoning happens directly on English sentences.
Write 'Marcus is a man' in predicate logic.
Using frames for a 'Car' with slots like colour, engine. Which concept?
Why do we need backward mapping?
knowledgeCheck.answer: To convert inferred internal results back into human-readable facts.

ai-c1-t11.quickRevision: AI representation is the way facts about the world are encoded in a form a program can store and reason with. Remember: Mapping diagram: Facts → Representation → Reasoning → Representation → Facts.

ai-c1-t12.title: Properties of Internal Representation
ai-c1-t12.definition: Properties of a good internal representation are representational adequacy, inferential adequacy, inferential efficiency and acquisitional efficiency.
ai-c1-t12.simpleExplanation: Achhi representation wahi hai jo sab zaroori facts rakh sake, naye facts nikaal sake, jaldi nikaal sake, aur naya knowledge aasani se add ho sake.
ai-c1-t12.realLifeAnalogy: A good filing system: it can hold every kind of document, help you derive what's missing, find files fast, and accept new files easily.
ai-c1-t12.example: Logic can represent 'all men are mortal' (adequate), derive new facts (inferential adequacy), but unrestricted logic can be slow (efficiency issue). Frames are efficient for default values but weak for complex logic.
keyPoints: Representational adequacy – can represent all required knowledge.
Inferential adequacy – can derive new knowledge from existing.
Inferential efficiency – can direct inference toward promising paths.
Acquisitional efficiency – new knowledge can be easily added.
No single scheme is best on all four.
mustKnow: Four properties by Rich & Knight with one-line meaning.
ifYouKnow: Name and explain the four properties.
commonMistakes: Mixing inferential adequacy (can derive) with inferential efficiency (derives quickly).
Believing the most expressive scheme is always best.

examQuestions.question: Explain properties of a good knowledge representation.
examQuestions.answer: Representational adequacy, inferential adequacy, inferential efficiency and acquisitional efficiency with one line each.

examQuestions.question: Inferential adequacy vs inferential efficiency.
examQuestions.answer: Adequacy: ability to derive new knowledge; efficiency: ability to do so quickly using guidance.

knowledgeCheck.question: Ability to add new knowledge easily is:
One scheme satisfies all four properties perfectly.

knowledgeCheck.answer: Ability to represent all kinds of knowledge needed in the domain.

knowledgeCheck.question: Inferential adequacy vs efficiency.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Adequacy = can infer; efficiency = infers fast with guidance.

ai-c1-t13.definition: The future scope of AI covers expected growth in capabilities, industries and responsibilities, from general intelligence research to ethical governance.

ai-c1-t13.realLifeAnalogy: AI today is like electricity in its early days: it is spreading everywhere and society must decide the rules.
ai-c1-t13.example: Autonomous vehicles reduce accidents; AI tutors personalise learning; AI in agriculture predicts crop disease from drone images.
keyPoints: Possible progress toward Artificial General Intelligence.

ai-c1-t14.title: Issues in the Design of Search Algorithms
ai-c1-t14.definition: Issues in search design are the choices and difficulties when designing a search: direction, rule selection, node representation, repeated states and the use of heuristics.
ai-c1-t14.simpleExplanation: Search banate waqt kuch sawal aate hain: aage se chalein ya goal se peeche? kaunsa rule chunein? same state dobara aaye to kya? Ye sab design issues hain.
ai-c1-t14.realLifeAnalogy: Finding a path in a maze: do you start from the entrance or the exit? Do you mark paths you've already visited? Those choices are design issues.
ai-c1-t14.example: 8-puzzle: forward search from the start board can be used; backward from the goal also works. If you don't remember visited boards, you may loop forever; a closed list avoids repeats.
keyPoints: Direction of search: forward, backward or bidirectional.
Selecting applicable rules efficiently (matching).
Representing each node of the search process.
Search tree vs graph: handling repeated states/loops.
Use of heuristics to guide search.
Performance criteria: completeness, optimality, time and space complexity.
mustKnow: Forward vs backward search when to prefer which.
ifYouKnow: Choose search direction for a problem.
commonMistakes: Assuming forward search is always best.
Ignoring repeated states, causing infinite loops.

examQuestions.question: Discuss issues in the design of search programs.
examQuestions.answer: Direction, rule selection, node representation, tree vs graph, heuristics, and performance (completeness, optimality, time, space).

examQuestions.question: Completeness vs optimality.
examQuestions.answer: Completeness: finds a solution if one exists; optimality: finds the best (least-cost) solution.

knowledgeCheck.question: Backward search is sometimes better than forward search.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: When goal is unique and branching backward is lower.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why keep a closed list?
knowledgeCheck.answer: To avoid revisiting the same states and looping.

knowledgeCheck.question: Many start states but one goal. Preferred direction?
Tree search vs graph search.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Tree search may revisit states; graph search tracks visited states.

ai-c1-t15.title: Introduction to AI Problems and Applications
ai-c1-t15.definition: AI problems and applications are real-world tasks, such as games, language, vision, robotics and diagnosis, that AI formulates as problems and solves with suitable techniques.
ai-c1-t15.simpleExplanation: Har real problem ko pehle AI problem ki tarah define karte hain (state, goal, actions), phir uski application banti hai - game, translation, face recognition, robot, diagnosis.
ai-c1-t15.realLifeAnalogy: Like turning a messy real-life task into a clean exam question before solving it.
ai-c1-t15.example: Game playing: state = board, actions = legal moves, goal = win. NLP: input sentence → output translated sentence. Robotics: state = position and sensor data, actions = motor commands, goal = reach target safely.
keyPoints: Games, theorem proving, NLP, computer vision, robotics, expert systems, speech.
Formulating a problem: states, actions, goal test, path cost.
Different applications need different techniques (search, learning, logic).
Real-world problems are noisy and uncertain.
ifYouKnow: Map an application to its AI area.
commonMistakes: Jumping to coding without formulating states/goals.
Using one technique for every application.

examQuestions.question: Explain AI problems and applications with examples.
examQuestions.answer: Game playing (search), NLP (parsing/translation), vision (recognition), robotics (planning/control), expert systems (rules).

knowledgeCheck.question: Robot must reach a target avoiding obstacles. Area?
What is a goal test?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A check whether a state satisfies the goal.
