ai-c1-t16.title: Defining Problems as a State Space Search
ai-c1-t16.definition: State space search formulates a problem as a set of states, an initial state, goal state(s), and operators; solving means finding a path from initial to goal.
ai-c1-t16.simpleExplanation: Problem ko states ka graph samjho. Start state se goal state tak operators (moves) lagakar pahunchna hai. Is graph ko search karna hi problem solving hai.
ai-c1-t16.realLifeAnalogy: Google Maps: each place is a state, each road is an operator, your location is the start and your destination is the goal. Finding the route is searching the state space.
ai-c1-t16.example: 8-puzzle: state = arrangement of tiles; initial = given board; goal = tiles in order; operators = move blank up/down/left/right; path cost = number of moves. Solution = sequence of blank moves reaching the goal.
keyPoints: Steps: define state space, initial state, goal state, operators/rules.
Also define path cost and goal test.
State space can be seen as a graph or tree.
Solution = path from initial to goal.
Good state representation keeps the space small.
Example problems: 8-puzzle, water jug, missionaries and cannibals, TSP.
mustKnow: Difference between state, operator and solution.
ifYouKnow: Formulate any puzzle as state space.
commonMistakes: Mixing the state (a configuration) with the operator (a move).
Forgetting a goal test or path cost in the formulation.

examQuestions.question: Explain defining a problem as state space search.
examQuestions.answer: Specify states, initial state, goal states, operators, goal test and path cost, then search for a path.

examQuestions.question: Formulate the 8-puzzle.
examQuestions.answer: State = tile arrangement; initial = given; goal = ordered; operators = move blank U/D/L/R; cost = 1 per move.

knowledgeCheck.question: In state space search, the solution is:
knowledgeCheck.answer: A path from initial to goal
options: A path from initial to goal

knowledgeCheck.question: Operators change one state into another.
What does path cost measure?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The total cost of operators applied along the path.

knowledgeCheck.question: Water jug 4L/3L: what is the initial state?
Route finding on a map: what are the states?

ai-c1-t16.quickRevision: State space search formulates a problem as a set of states, an initial state, goal state(s), and operators; solving means finding a path from initial to goal. Remember: Four-step formulation.

ai-c2-t01.title: Generate-And-Test
ai-c2-t01.definition: Generate-and-Test is a search method that repeatedly generates a candidate solution and tests whether it satisfies the goal, stopping when a test succeeds.
ai-c2-t01.simpleExplanation: Sabse simple idea: ek possible answer banao, check karo sahi hai ya nahi. Galat hai to agla banao. Isme koi smart guidance nahi hoti, bas generate aur test.
ai-c2-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Trying keys one by one on a locked door: pick a key (generate), try it (test), repeat until the door opens.
ai-c2-t01.example: Four-digit PIN lock: generate 0000, 0001, 0002… test each against the lock. Works but takes up to 10,000 tries.
keyPoints: Two modules: generator and tester.
Exhaustive generation = British Museum / brute-force; guarantees a solution if one exists in a finite space.
Systematic generation avoids repeats; random generation may repeat.
Tester only answers yes/no; it gives no direction.
Works well only for small search spaces.
Improved by Plan–Generate–Test: a planner prunes candidates first (DENDRAL).
mustKnow: It is like depth-first search when generation is systematic.
commonMistakes: Thinking the tester guides the generator — in pure G&T it does not.
Assuming it is efficient; it is exponential in general.
Confusing random G&T (may repeat, no guarantee) with systematic G&T.

examQuestions.question: Explain Generate-and-Test with algorithm.
examQuestions.answer: Generate a possible solution; test if it is a goal; if yes stop, else repeat.

examQuestions.question: Generate-and-test vs hill climbing.
examQuestions.answer: G&T tester gives only yes/no; hill climbing uses the test result as heuristic feedback to choose the next state.

examQuestions.question: What is the main drawback?
examQuestions.answer: Exponential time because it may examine the whole search space with no guidance.

knowledgeCheck.question: In pure Generate-and-Test the tester gives:
G&T is efficient for large search spaces.
Name the two modules of G&T.
A 3-digit lock (000–999). Worst-case number of tests?
Systematic vs random generation.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Systematic never repeats and is complete; random may repeat and has no guarantee.

knowledgeCheck.question: How can G&T be made smarter?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Prune candidates with a planner or constraints before generating (Plan-Generate-Test).

algorithmSteps: 1. Generate a possible solution (a state or a path).
2. Test whether it is a goal state.
3. If yes → return it and stop.
4. Otherwise → go to step 1.
ai-c2-t01.stateSpace: State = any candidate solution; no operators needed beyond the generator; goal test = tester.
ai-c2-t01.complexity: Time O(b^d) worst case (all candidates); Space O(1) for random, O(d) for DFS-like systematic generation.
ai-c2-t01.quickRevision: Generate-and-Test is a search method that repeatedly generates a candidate solution and tests whether it satisfies the goal, stopping when a test succeeds. Remember: Three-step algorithm.

ai-c2-t02.title: Hill Climbing
ai-c2-t02.definition: Hill climbing is a local search that moves from the current state to a neighbouring state with a better heuristic value, stopping when no neighbour is better.
ai-c2-t02.simpleExplanation: Fog me pahaad chadhne jaisa: jo nearby step upar le jaye wahi chalo. Door ka nahi dekhte, sirf aas-paas ka. Isliye kabhi chhoti pahadi (local maximum) pe atak jaate hain.
ai-c2-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Climbing a mountain in thick fog and always stepping to the highest nearby ground; you may end up on a small hill, thinking it is the top.
ai-c2-t02.example: Heights along a path: A=2, B=5, C=8, D=6. Start at A → B → C. At C neighbours (B=5, D=6) are lower, so stop at C. If a taller peak existed far away, we would miss it: C is a local maximum.
keyPoints: Uses an evaluation function; moves to a better neighbour only.
Keeps no search tree/history → very low memory.
Simple HC: first better neighbour; Steepest-ascent: best neighbour; Stochastic: random better neighbour.
Problems: local maxima, plateau, ridge.
Remedies: random restarts, backtracking, bigger jumps, moving in several directions.
Not complete and not optimal.
mustKnow: Three problems and one remedy each.
ifYouKnow: Run hill climbing on a small example.
commonMistakes: Believing it always finds the global optimum.
Mixing plateau (flat area) with ridge (sequence of local maxima hard to climb).
Forgetting hill climbing stores only the current node.

examQuestions.question: Explain hill climbing with algorithm and problems.
examQuestions.answer: Algorithm below; problems: local maximum, plateau, ridge; fixes: random restart, backtracking, larger steps.

examQuestions.question: Simple hill climbing vs steepest-ascent.
examQuestions.answer: Simple takes the first better neighbour; steepest-ascent evaluates all neighbours and picks the best.

examQuestions.question: Hill climbing vs best-first search.
examQuestions.answer: Hill climbing keeps only the current state and never backtracks; best-first keeps an OPEN list and can return to earlier nodes.

examQuestions.question: Why is its memory requirement small?
examQuestions.answer: It stores only the current state and its neighbours.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is a problem of hill climbing?
What is a plateau?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A flat region where neighbouring states have equal value, so there is no direction to move.

knowledgeCheck.question: Values A=2,B=5,C=8,D=6 along a line, start at B. Where does HC stop?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: C's neighbours B=5, D=6 are lower.

knowledgeCheck.question: Random restart hill climbing helps with…
knowledgeCheck.answer: Escaping local maxima by trying many start states.

knowledgeCheck.question: A robot's HC search stops on a small peak. Which remedy?

algorithmSteps: 1. Set current = initial state; if it is a goal, stop.
2. Generate the neighbours of current.
3. Evaluate neighbours with the heuristic.
4. If the best neighbour is better than current → current = that neighbour; go to step 2.
5. Otherwise stop (no better neighbour); return current.
ai-c2-t02.stateSpace: Landscape of states with an objective function; operators move to neighbouring states; goal = maximum value.
ai-c2-t02.complexity: Time O(m·b) for m steps and b neighbours; Space O(1) (current state only).
ai-c2-t02.workedExample: Maximise f on positions 0–4 with f = [2,5,8,6,9]. Start at 0: 2→5→8; neighbour 6 is lower → stop at 8 (position 2). The global maximum 9 at position 4 is missed ⇒ local maximum.
ai-c2-t02.quickRevision: Hill climbing is a local search that moves from the current state to a neighbouring state with a better heuristic value, stopping when no neighbour is better. Remember: Algorithm steps.

ai-c2-t03.title: Best-First Search
ai-c2-t03.definition: Best-first search expands the most promising node from an OPEN list ordered by an evaluation function, combining the advantages of depth-first and breadth-first search.
ai-c2-t03.simpleExplanation: Har step pe wo node expand karo jo goal ke sabse paas lagta hai (heuristic ke hisaab se). Hill climbing ke opposite, yahan purane nodes yaad rehte hain isliye backtrack ho sakta hai.
ai-c2-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Choosing which restaurant queue to join by always picking the one that looks shortest at the moment, while remembering the other queues in case this one stalls.
ai-c2-t03.example: Heuristic h: S=7, A=5, B=3, C=2, D=4, G=0. Edges: S→A, S→B, B→C, B→D, C→G. OPEN={S}. Expand S: A(5), B(3). Pick B(3): add C(2), D(4). Pick C(2): add G(0). Pick G → goal. Path S–B–C–G.
keyPoints: Uses OPEN (priority queue) and CLOSED lists.
Greedy best-first: f(n)=h(n).
Works on OR graphs (many ways to reach the same node).
Can backtrack to a better earlier node via OPEN.
Not optimal; not always complete (infinite loops without CLOSED).
Time and space O(b^m) worst case.
ifYouKnow: Trace best-first on a small tree.
Explain difference from hill climbing and A*.
commonMistakes: Calling it optimal — it ignores the cost so far g(n).
Forgetting to check CLOSED, which causes repeated expansion.
Thinking it is the same as BFS (it uses a heuristic, not level order).

examQuestions.question: Explain best-first search with algorithm.
examQuestions.answer: OPEN list ordered by h(n); repeatedly expand best node until goal.

examQuestions.question: Best-first vs hill climbing.
examQuestions.answer: Best-first keeps OPEN and can backtrack; hill climbing keeps only the current state.

examQuestions.question: Is greedy best-first optimal?
examQuestions.answer: No, it ignores path cost so far.

knowledgeCheck.question: What data structure holds OPEN?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A priority queue ordered by heuristic.

knowledgeCheck.question: OPEN has A(h=5), B(h=3), D(h=4). Which node is expanded?
Best-first vs BFS.
knowledgeCheck.answer: BFS expands by depth; best-first expands by heuristic value.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why use CLOSED?
knowledgeCheck.answer: To avoid re-expanding visited nodes and looping.

algorithmSteps: 1. Put the start node on OPEN with its h value; CLOSED = empty.
2. If OPEN is empty → fail.
3. Remove the node n with the lowest h from OPEN; move it to CLOSED.
4. If n is a goal → return the path.
5. Generate successors; for each not in OPEN/CLOSED compute h, set parent = n, add to OPEN.
6. Go to step 2.
ai-c2-t03.stateSpace: OR graph of states; evaluation function f(n)=h(n); OPEN = frontier, CLOSED = expanded.
ai-c2-t03.complexity: Time O(b^m), Space O(b^m) in the worst case (m = max depth); good heuristic reduces this a lot.

comparison.title: Best-First vs Hill Climbing vs A*

ai-c2-t03.quickRevision: Best-first search expands the most promising node from an OPEN list ordered by an evaluation function, combining the advantages of depth-first and breadth-first search. Remember: Algorithm with OPEN/CLOSED.

ai-c2-t04.title: Problem Reduction
ai-c2-t04.definition: Problem reduction solves a problem by decomposing it into sub-problems, represented on an AND-OR graph where AND arcs need all sub-problems solved and OR arcs need any one.
ai-c2-t04.simpleExplanation: Bade problem ko chhote problems me todo. AND ka matlab saare chhote kaam karne padenge, OR ka matlab koi ek raasta chal jayega.
ai-c2-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Making a project report: it is AND (write + diagrams + conclusion all needed), but for getting a laptop it is OR (borrow OR buy).
ai-c2-t04.example: Goal: Acquire a TV. OR: Steal a TV, OR [AND: Earn money, Buy a TV]. Solution graph picks the cheapest valid choice; the AND branch costs earn + buy.
keyPoints: Represented as an AND-OR graph.
AND arc: all successors must be solved.
OR arc: any one successor suffices.
Solution is a subgraph, not a single path.
Cost of AND arc = sum of costs of its children.
Algorithm for it: AO*.
Examples: symbolic integration, Tower of Hanoi, theorem proving.
mustKnow: Difference between AND and OR nodes.
ifYouKnow: Explain why normal best-first fails here.
commonMistakes: Treating the solution as a single path; it is a subgraph.
Adding costs of OR children — only the best OR choice counts.

examQuestions.question: Explain problem reduction with AND-OR graph.
examQuestions.answer: Decompose into sub-problems; AND arcs need all, OR arcs need one; solution is a subgraph.

examQuestions.question: Show 'Acquire TV' as AND-OR graph.
examQuestions.answer: Root OR: Steal | AND(Earn money, Buy TV).

examQuestions.question: Why is best-first search unsuitable here?
examQuestions.answer: It handles OR graphs only and cannot represent AND dependencies.

knowledgeCheck.question: A solution to an AND-OR graph is always a single path.
AND arc to X(cost 3) and Y(cost 4), arc costs 1 each. Total?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: (3+1)+(4+1)=9 with per-arc cost added to each child.

knowledgeCheck.question: Choose between two plans: one OR option costs 6, another AND option costs 3+2. Best?

algorithmSteps: 1. Represent the problem as the root of an AND-OR graph.
2. Expand a node into sub-problems (AND set or OR alternatives).
3. Estimate the cost of each arc; AND arc cost = sum of children.
4. Select the cheapest arc for each node; build the current best solution graph.
5. Repeat until every node of the solution graph is solved (primitive).
ai-c2-t04.stateSpace: AND-OR graph: nodes = problems, OR arcs = alternatives, AND arcs = sub-problem sets.
ai-c2-t04.quickRevision: Problem reduction solves a problem by decomposing it into sub-problems, represented on an AND-OR graph where AND arcs need all sub-problems solved and OR arcs need any one. Remember: Difference between AND and OR nodes.

ai-c2-t05.title: Constraint Satisfaction
ai-c2-t05.definition: A Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) assigns values to variables from their domains so that all constraints are satisfied.
ai-c2-t05.simpleExplanation: Kuch variables hain, har ek ke liye allowed values hain aur kuch rules (constraints) hain. Aisi assignment dhundni hai jo sab rules maane.
ai-c2-t05.realLifeAnalogy: Making an exam timetable: each exam (variable) gets a slot (value), and no two exams of the same student can clash (constraint).
ai-c2-t05.example: Cryptarithmetic SEND+MORE=MONEY. Reasoning: M=1 (carry), O=0, S=9 → solution S=9,E=5,N=6,D=7,M=1,O=0,R=8,Y=2: 9567+1085=10652 ✓.
keyPoints: Defined by variables, domains and constraints.
Solving = constraint propagation + guessing with backtracking.
Examples: map colouring, N-Queens, cryptarithmetic, Sudoku.
Constraint propagation narrows domains before guessing.
Heuristics: minimum remaining values, most constraining variable.
Backtracking worst case O(d^n).
commonMistakes: Guessing values before propagating constraints.
Forgetting constraints like 'all letters different'.

examQuestions.question: Explain constraint satisfaction with example.
examQuestions.answer: Variables, domains, constraints; propagate constraints, guess if stuck, backtrack on conflict; solve SEND+MORE=MONEY.

examQuestions.question: Colour a triangle graph with 3 colours.
examQuestions.answer: Assign distinct colours to the 3 nodes.

examQuestions.question: How does CSP improve generate-and-test?
examQuestions.answer: It prunes invalid partial assignments early using constraints.

knowledgeCheck.question: Propagation vs guessing.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Propagation logically deduces; guessing tries a value and backtracks if it fails.

algorithmSteps: 1. Initialise variables with their domains and constraints.
2. Propagate: apply constraints to reduce domains or fix variables.
3. If all variables are assigned and constraints hold → solution.
4. If a domain becomes empty → backtrack.
5. Otherwise pick an unassigned variable, guess a value, and go to step 2.
ai-c2-t05.stateSpace: State = partial assignment of variables; operator = assign a value; goal = complete consistent assignment.
ai-c2-t05.complexity: Backtracking worst case O(d^n); propagation and heuristics give large practical savings.
ai-c2-t05.quickRevision: A Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) assigns values to variables from their domains so that all constraints are satisfied. Remember: Three CSP components.

ai-c2-t06.title: Means-Ends Analysis
ai-c2-t06.definition: Means-ends analysis reduces the difference between the current state and the goal by choosing an operator that removes that difference, creating sub-goals when its preconditions are unmet.
ai-c2-t06.simpleExplanation: Current state aur goal ke beech ka difference dekho, phir wo operator chuno jo is difference ko kam kare. Agar operator abhi apply nahi ho sakta, to uski shart pehle poori karne ka sub-goal banao.
ai-c2-t06.realLifeAnalogy: To reach Mumbai from college: difference = distance; operator = train. Train needs a ticket (precondition), so first solve the sub-problem 'get a ticket'.
ai-c2-t06.example: Go from home to airport. Difference: location. Operator: taxi. Precondition: book a taxi → sub-goal. After it, difference is gone. Solved by chaining operators. This is how GPS (General Problem Solver) works.
keyPoints: Used in General Problem Solver (Newell & Simon).
Combines forward and backward reasoning.
Uses a difference table linking differences to operators.
Operator preconditions create sub-goals.
Recursive: reduce difference → solve preconditions → apply operator.
Used in planning.
commonMistakes: Choosing operators randomly instead of by difference.
Ignoring preconditions of operators.

examQuestions.question: Explain means-ends analysis.
examQuestions.answer: Find difference; select operator reducing it; if preconditions fail, create sub-goal; apply and repeat.

examQuestions.question: Which system used MEA?
examQuestions.answer: General Problem Solver (GPS).

knowledgeCheck.question: MEA reduces:
knowledgeCheck.answer: Difference between current and goal state
options: Difference between current and goal state

knowledgeCheck.question: MEA creates sub-goals when operator preconditions fail.
What is a difference table?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A table mapping differences to operators that can reduce them.

knowledgeCheck.question: You need to pay but lack cash. Sub-goal?
MEA vs forward search.
knowledgeCheck.answer: MEA is goal-directed using differences; forward search expands states blindly.

algorithmSteps: 1. Compare CURRENT and GOAL; if no difference → success.
2. Select the most important difference D.
3. Choose an operator O that reduces D.
4. If O's preconditions are not satisfied in CURRENT → solve that as a sub-problem (recursive MEA).
5. Apply O to get a new CURRENT; go to step 1.
ai-c2-t06.stateSpace: State descriptions; operators with preconditions and effects; difference table.
ai-c2-t06.workedExample: Start: at home without ticket. Goal: in Mumbai. D = location. O = train. Precondition 'have ticket' unmet → sub-goal get ticket (operator: buy online) → apply; then travel.
ai-c2-t06.quickRevision: Means-ends analysis reduces the difference between the current state and the goal by choosing an operator that removes that difference, creating sub-goals when its preconditions are unmet. Remember: Four steps of MEA.

ai-c2-t07.title: Heuristic Search
ai-c2-t07.definition: Heuristic search uses a heuristic function h(n), an estimate of the cost from node n to the goal, to guide the search towards promising states.
ai-c2-t07.simpleExplanation: Heuristic ek smart guess hai ki goal kitna door hai. Is guess se search ko sahi direction milti hai, to har rasta try nahi karna padta.
ai-c2-t07.realLifeAnalogy: Using the 'distance to destination' shown on a signboard to decide which road to take, even though you are not sure of the exact route.
ai-c2-t07.example: 8-puzzle start 2 8 3 / 1 6 4 / 7 _ 5, goal 1 2 3 / 8 _ 4 / 7 6 5. h1 = misplaced tiles = 4 (2,8,1,6). h2 = Manhattan distance = 1+2+1+1 = 5. h2 ≥ h1, so h2 is more informed.
keyPoints: h(n) estimates the cheapest cost from n to a goal; h(goal)=0.
Admissible: never overestimates the true cost.
Consistent: h(n) ≤ cost(n,n') + h(n').
8-puzzle heuristics: misplaced tiles, Manhattan distance.
More informed heuristic (dominates) expands fewer nodes.
Trade-off: accuracy vs time to compute.
Heuristics trade completeness/optimality for speed in some methods.
ifYouKnow: Compute misplaced tiles and Manhattan distance.
commonMistakes: Using a heuristic that overestimates and expecting optimal A*.
Thinking a heuristic gives the exact cost.
Counting the blank tile in misplaced tiles.

examQuestions.question: What is a heuristic? What makes it admissible?
examQuestions.answer: An estimate of cost to goal; admissible means it never overestimates the real cost.

examQuestions.question: Compute h1 and h2 for the given 8-puzzle.
Why is Manhattan distance better than misplaced tiles?
examQuestions.answer: It is also admissible and larger (more informed), so fewer nodes are expanded.

knowledgeCheck.question: A tile is 2 rows up and 1 column left of its goal. Manhattan contribution?
Informed vs uninformed search.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Informed uses a heuristic to guide; uninformed uses only the problem definition.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is dominance of heuristics?
knowledgeCheck.answer: If h2(n) ≥ h1(n) for all n (both admissible), h2 dominates and is better.

ai-c2-t07.stateSpace: 8-puzzle state = 3×3 arrangement; operators = move blank; h(n) = estimated moves to goal.
ai-c2-t07.quickRevision: Heuristic search uses a heuristic function h(n), an estimate of the cost from node n to the goal, to guide the search towards promising states. Remember: Admissible and consistent definitions.

ai-c2-t08.title: A* and AO* Algorithm
ai-c2-t08.definition: A* finds a least-cost path using f(n)=g(n)+h(n); AO* is its counterpart for AND-OR graphs, finding the minimum-cost solution graph.
ai-c2-t08.simpleExplanation: A* har node ke liye 'ab tak ka cost + goal tak ka estimate' dekhta hai aur sabse chhota f wala expand karta hai. AO* wahi idea AND-OR graph pe lagata hai.
ai-c2-t08.realLifeAnalogy: A* is like planning a trip using both what you have already spent (g) and the predicted remaining cost (h). AO* is planning a project where some tasks must all be done (AND).
ai-c2-t08.example: Edges: S→A(1), S→B(4), A→G(10), B→G(3). h: S=6, A=9, B=3, G=0. Expand S: f(A)=1+9=10, f(B)=4+3=7. Pick B: G has g=7,f=7. Pick G (7<10). Path S–B–G cost 7.
keyPoints: Optimal and complete if h is admissible (tree) / consistent (graph).
Space is its biggest problem: O(b^d).
A* with h=0 is uniform-cost search; with g=0 it is greedy best-first.
AO* works on AND-OR graphs; cost of AND arc = sum of children + arc costs.
AO* revises costs backwards (cost propagation) and marks nodes SOLVED.
mustKnow: AO* steps: expand, revise cost, mark solved.
commonMistakes: Using a non-admissible heuristic and still claiming optimality.
Forgetting g(n) — that gives greedy search.
Thinking AO* handles only OR graphs.

examQuestions.question: Trace A* on S–A–B–G graph above.
examQuestions.answer: Pick B (f=7) then G (f=7); cost 7.

examQuestions.question: Explain AO* algorithm.
examQuestions.answer: Pick the current best partial solution graph, expand an unexpanded node, compute costs of its arcs, propagate revised cost upward, mark SOLVED nodes, repeat until root solved.

examQuestions.question: A* vs AO*.
examQuestions.answer: A* searches OR graphs for a path; AO* searches AND-OR graphs for a solution graph.

examQuestions.question: When is A* optimal?
examQuestions.answer: When h is admissible (and consistent for graph search).

knowledgeCheck.question: A* is optimal with an admissible heuristic.
What is the main drawback of A*?
What does AO* do after expanding a node?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Recomputes costs and propagates them back towards the root.

algorithmSteps: A*: 1. OPEN={start}, g(start)=0, f=h(start); CLOSED={}.
2. If OPEN empty → fail.
3. Remove n with least f from OPEN; add to CLOSED.
4. If n is goal → return path via parents.
5. For each successor m: g'=g(n)+cost; if m is new or g' is smaller → set parent, g, f=g+h and put/update in OPEN.
6. Repeat from step 2.
AO*: 1. Start with the root as the current solution graph.
2. Choose an unexpanded node of the best current solution graph and expand it.
3. For new nodes compute h; for each AND/OR arc compute cost; choose the minimum.
4. Propagate the revised cost to ancestors; mark nodes SOLVED when all required children are solved.
5. Stop when the root is SOLVED (or its cost exceeds a futility limit).
ai-c2-t08.stateSpace: A*: OR graph, f=g+h. AO*: AND-OR graph, solution = subgraph.
ai-c2-t08.complexity: A*: Time O(b^d) worst, Space O(b^d); a good heuristic reduces the effective branching factor. AO*: also exponential worst case.
ai-c2-t08.quickRevision: A* finds a least-cost path using f(n)=g(n)+h(n); AO* is its counterpart for AND-OR graphs, finding the minimum-cost solution graph. Remember: A* algorithm steps.

ai-c2-t09.title: Knowledge Representation: Basic Concepts
ai-c2-t09.definition: Knowledge representation (KR) is the study of how facts, rules and relationships about the world are encoded so that a program can store and reason with them.
ai-c2-t09.simpleExplanation: Reasoning ke liye pehle knowledge ko sahi form me store karna padta hai. Facts, rules aur relationships ko organise karna hi KR hai.
ai-c2-t09.realLifeAnalogy: A library catalogue: books (facts) are stored with categories and links so a librarian can quickly find answers.
ai-c2-t09.example: Declarative: 'Tom is a cat.' Procedural: 'steps to make tea.' Heuristic: 'if a patient has fever and rash, suspect measles first.' All can be stored in a KR system.
keyPoints: Knowledge types: declarative, procedural, heuristic, meta-knowledge, structural.
Data → Information → Knowledge hierarchy.
KR needs: representational adequacy, inferential adequacy and efficiency, acquisitional efficiency.
KR components: knowledge base + inference mechanism.
KR can be logical, rule-based, network-based or frame-based.
Facts are mapped to a representation, reasoning applied, results mapped back.
mustKnow: Requirements of a good KR scheme.
ifYouKnow: Explain components of a KR system.
commonMistakes: Confusing data with knowledge.
Thinking KR is just a database; it supports inference.

examQuestions.question: Define knowledge representation and list its types of knowledge.
examQuestions.answer: Encoding knowledge for reasoning; types: declarative, procedural, heuristic, meta, structural.

examQuestions.question: Declarative vs procedural knowledge.
examQuestions.answer: Declarative states facts (what); procedural describes how to do things.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is meta-knowledge?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Knowledge about knowledge, such as how reliable or when to use a rule.

knowledgeCheck.question: 'If fever and rash, suspect measles.' Which type?
Two parts of a knowledge-based system?

ai-c2-t09.quickRevision: Knowledge representation (KR) is the study of how facts, rules and relationships about the world are encoded so that a program can store and reason with them. Remember: Types of knowledge with examples.

ai-c2-t10.title: Knowledge Representation Paradigms
ai-c2-t10.definition: KR paradigms are the main ways to encode knowledge: logic, semantic networks, frames and production rules.
ai-c2-t10.simpleExplanation: Knowledge likhne ke alag-alag tareeke hote hain: logic (formal), semantic net (graph), frames (slots), rules (IF-THEN). Har ke apne fayde aur limits hain.
ai-c2-t10.realLifeAnalogy: Same information can be a sentence, a mind map, a form with fields or a rulebook, each good for different uses.
ai-c2-t10.example: 'Tom is a cat; cats are mammals.' Logic: cat(Tom), ∀x cat(x)→mammal(x). Semantic net: Tom –instance→ Cat –isa→ Mammal. Frame: Cat{isa: Mammal}, Tom{instance: Cat}. Rule: IF cat(x) THEN mammal(x).
keyPoints: Logical: propositional and predicate logic; precise, supports sound inference.
Semantic networks: nodes and labelled arcs; intuitive; inheritance.
Frames: slot–filler structures with defaults; good for stereotypes.
Production rules: IF–THEN; modular; used in expert systems.
Others: scripts, conceptual dependency, ontologies.
No single paradigm is best; choose by the domain.
mustKnow: Four paradigms with a one-line strength/weakness.
ifYouKnow: Choose a paradigm for a scenario.
commonMistakes: Thinking semantic nets have formal semantics like logic (they are informal).
Choosing logic for everything though it can be slow.

examQuestions.question: Explain KR paradigms with examples.
examQuestions.answer: Logic, semantic network, frames, production rules; show 'Tom is a cat' in each.

examQuestions.question: Semantic network vs frames.
examQuestions.answer: Semantic nets are graphs of nodes/links; frames group attributes into slots with defaults and procedures.

knowledgeCheck.question: Strength of logic?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Precise, unambiguous and supports sound inference.

knowledgeCheck.question: Expert system for diagnosis likely uses…
Logic vs semantic net.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Logic is formal and precise; semantic net is intuitive but informal.

ai-c2-t10.quickRevision: KR paradigms are the main ways to encode knowledge: logic, semantic networks, frames and production rules. Remember: Four paradigms with a one-line strength/weakness.

ai-c2-t11.title: Propositional Logic
ai-c2-t11.definition: Propositional logic is a formal language of declarative statements (propositions) that are either true or false, combined using connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔.
ai-c2-t11.simpleExplanation: Propositional logic me har statement ya to true hota hai ya false. Un statements ko AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN se jodkar naye statements bante hain.
ai-c2-t11.realLifeAnalogy: Like a light switch: each proposition is on or off and connectives describe how combined switches behave.
ai-c2-t11.example: P = 'It is raining', Q = 'I carry an umbrella'. P→Q says: if it rains then I carry an umbrella. Truth table of P→Q: false only when P=T and Q=F.
keyPoints: Atomic proposition: a statement that is true or false.
Connectives: ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (implies), ↔ (iff).
Tautology: always true; contradiction: always false; contingency: sometimes.
Equivalences: P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q; De Morgan: ¬(P∧Q) ≡ ¬P∨¬Q.
Satisfiable, valid and entailment (KB ⊨ α).
Limitation: cannot express 'all' or 'some' or relationships between objects.
commonMistakes: Thinking P→Q is false when P is false (it is true).
Mixing → with ↔.
Assuming PL can express 'All men are mortal' compactly.

examQuestions.question: Explain propositional logic with syntax and connectives.
examQuestions.answer: Propositions, connectives, truth tables, equivalences.

examQuestions.question: Prove P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q using a truth table.
examQuestions.answer: Both columns are F only when P=T,Q=F; otherwise T.

examQuestions.question: What is a tautology?
examQuestions.answer: A formula true under every interpretation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which connective represents 'if and only if'?
Tautology vs contradiction.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Tautology always true; contradiction always false.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is PL weak for real knowledge?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No variables or quantifiers, so general statements need many propositions.

ai-c2-t11.workedExample: Truth table for P→Q: (T,T)=T, (T,F)=F, (F,T)=T, (F,F)=T. ¬P∨Q gives the same column ⇒ P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q.
ai-c2-t11.quickRevision: Propositional logic is a formal language of declarative statements (propositions) that are either true or false, combined using connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔. Remember: Truth tables of →.

ai-c2-t12.title: Inference Rules in Propositional Logic
ai-c2-t12.definition: Inference rules are patterns that let us derive new valid propositional formulas from known ones, such as Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens.
ai-c2-t12.simpleExplanation: Inference rules ready-made reasoning patterns hain jo jaante hue facts se naya sach nikalte hain, bina truth table banaye.
ai-c2-t12.realLifeAnalogy: Like grammar rules for thinking: if 'all A are B' and 'x is A', you may safely conclude 'x is B'.
ai-c2-t12.example: Given P→Q, Q→R, P. By Modus Ponens P→Q, P ⊢ Q. Then Q→R, Q ⊢ R. So R is derived.
keyPoints: Modus Ponens (MP): P→Q, P ⊢ Q.
Modus Tollens (MT): P→Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P.
Hypothetical Syllogism (HS): P→Q, Q→R ⊢ P→R.
Disjunctive Syllogism (DS): P∨Q, ¬P ⊢ Q.
Addition: P ⊢ P∨Q.   Simplification: P∧Q ⊢ P.   Conjunction: P, Q ⊢ P∧Q.
Resolution: P∨Q, ¬P∨R ⊢ Q∨R.
ifYouKnow: Apply MP/MT/HS to derive a conclusion.
Identify the rule used in a step.
commonMistakes: Using the converse: from P→Q and Q conclude P (affirming the consequent is invalid).
Mixing MT with MP.

examQuestions.question: State and explain inference rules of propositional logic.
examQuestions.answer: MP, MT, HS, DS, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, Resolution with examples.

examQuestions.question: From P→Q, Q→R, ¬R derive ¬P.
examQuestions.answer: MT on Q→R,¬R gives ¬Q; MT on P→Q,¬Q gives ¬P.

examQuestions.question: Is 'P→Q, Q ⊢ P' valid?
examQuestions.answer: No — fallacy of affirming the consequent.

knowledgeCheck.question: P→Q and P gives Q by:
MP vs MT.
knowledgeCheck.answer: MP affirms the antecedent to get the consequent; MT denies the consequent to deny the antecedent.

algorithmSteps: 1. Write all premises as formulas.
2. Match a premise pattern with a rule.
3. Add the conclusion as a new line with its justification.
4. Repeat until the target formula appears.
ai-c2-t12.workedExample: Premises: 1) P→Q 2) Q→R 3) P. Steps: 4) Q (MP 1,3) 5) R (MP 2,4). Conclusion R.
ai-c2-t12.quickRevision: Inference rules are patterns that let us derive new valid propositional formulas from known ones, such as Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens. Remember: Seven standard rules.

ai-c2-t13.title: Knowledge Representation using Predicate Logic
ai-c2-t13.definition: Predicate (first-order) logic represents knowledge with objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers, allowing statements about all or some objects.
ai-c2-t13.simpleExplanation: Predicate logic me hum objects aur unke relations likhte hain, jaise man(Marcus). ∀ (sabke liye) aur ∃ (kuch ke liye) se general facts bhi likh sakte hain.
ai-c2-t13.realLifeAnalogy: Like an Excel sheet with columns (predicates) and rows (objects), plus formulas that apply to every row.
ai-c2-t13.example: Marcus facts: man(Marcus); Pompeian(Marcus); ∀x Pompeian(x)→Roman(x); ruler(Caesar); ∀x Roman(x)→loyalto(x,Caesar) ∨ hate(x,Caesar); tryassassinate(Marcus,Caesar). Query: was Marcus loyal to Caesar? — reasoning leads to hate(Marcus,Caesar).
keyPoints: Symbols: constants, variables, functions, predicates, connectives, quantifiers.
∀ usually pairs with →; ∃ usually pairs with ∧.
Facts become well-formed formulas (WFFs).
Can represent classes: ∀x man(x)→mortal(x).
Can represent instance and isa relationships.
More expressive than propositional logic, but not decidable in general.
mustKnow: Why it is more powerful than PL.
ifYouKnow: Translate English sentences to predicate logic.
commonMistakes: Writing ∀x (man(x) ∧ mortal(x)) for 'all men are mortal' — it should be →.
Writing ∃x (man(x) → mortal(x)) for 'some man is mortal' — it should be ∧.

examQuestions.question: Represent facts using predicate logic.
examQuestions.answer: man(Marcus), ∀x man(x)→mortal(x) etc.

examQuestions.question: Propositional vs predicate logic.
examQuestions.answer: Predicate logic has objects, predicates, variables and quantifiers; propositional logic has only whole propositions.

knowledgeCheck.question: Constant vs variable.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Constant names a specific object; variable stands for any object.

ai-c2-t13.workedExample: 'All Pompeians were Romans' → ∀x Pompeian(x)→Roman(x). With Pompeian(Marcus), instantiate x=Marcus and apply Modus Ponens ⇒ Roman(Marcus).
ai-c2-t13.quickRevision: Predicate (first-order) logic represents knowledge with objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers, allowing statements about all or some objects. Remember: Marcus example.

ai-c2-t14.title: Predicate Calculus
ai-c2-t14.definition: Predicate calculus is the formal system of first-order logic: its syntax of terms and well-formed formulas, quantifiers and rules of inference and interpretation.
ai-c2-t14.simpleExplanation: Predicate calculus predicate logic ka formal system hai: kaise formulas likhte hain (syntax), unka matlab kya hai (semantics) aur proofs kaise hote hain.
ai-c2-t14.realLifeAnalogy: A grammar plus a dictionary: syntax says what sentences are well formed, semantics says what they mean in a world.
ai-c2-t14.example: Term: father(Ram). Atomic formula: loves(father(Ram), Sita). With quantifier: ∀x ∃y loves(x,y). Negation: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
keyPoints: Terms: constants, variables, function applications.
Atomic formula: predicate applied to terms.
WFFs built with connectives and quantifiers.
Free vs bound variables; a sentence has no free variables.
Quantifier negation: ¬∀x P ≡ ∃x¬P; ¬∃x P ≡ ∀x¬P.
Interpretation = domain + meaning of symbols; formula valid if true in all.
commonMistakes: Confusing predicate (true/false) with function (returns object).
Missing that variables in the scope of ∀ are bound.

examQuestions.question: Explain syntax and semantics of predicate calculus.
examQuestions.answer: Terms, atoms, WFFs, quantifiers, interpretation.

examQuestions.question: Negate ∀x P(x).
examQuestions.answer: ∃x ¬P(x)

knowledgeCheck.question: A sentence has no free variables.
Difference between function and predicate?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A function returns an object; a predicate returns true/false.

knowledgeCheck.question: In ∀x P(x,y), which variable is free?
∀ vs ∃.
knowledgeCheck.answer: ∀ means for all objects; ∃ means for at least one object.

ai-c2-t14.quickRevision: Predicate calculus is the formal system of first-order logic: its syntax of terms and well-formed formulas, quantifiers and rules of inference and interpretation. Remember: Syntax levels: term → atom → WFF.

ai-c2-t15.title: Predicate and Arguments
ai-c2-t15.definition: A predicate is a relation or property symbol applied to a fixed number of arguments (terms); the number of arguments is its arity.
ai-c2-t15.simpleExplanation: Predicate batata hai kisi object ka property ya objects ke beech relation, aur arguments wo objects hote hain. Jaise loves(Ram, Sita) me loves predicate hai, Ram aur Sita arguments.
ai-c2-t15.realLifeAnalogy: Like a function signature: loves(a, b) needs exactly two inputs and returns true or false.
ai-c2-t15.example: man(Marcus) — arity 1. loves(Ram,Sita) — arity 2. between(a,b,c) — arity 3. Order matters: loves(Ram,Sita) ≠ loves(Sita,Ram). Nested: older(father(Ram), Ram).
keyPoints: Arity = number of arguments.
Arguments can be constants, variables or functions.
Argument order matters.
Predicate returns true/false; function returns an object.
Unary predicates = properties; n-ary = relations.
Consistent argument order must be used throughout a knowledge base.
commonMistakes: Swapping argument order inconsistently.
Using a predicate where a function (returning an object) is needed.

examQuestions.question: What are predicates and arguments?
examQuestions.answer: Predicate: relation/property symbol; arguments: the terms it relates.

examQuestions.question: Is father(Ram) a predicate or function?
examQuestions.answer: Function; it denotes an object.

knowledgeCheck.question: loves(Ram,Sita) and loves(Sita,Ram) mean the same.
'Ram is taller than Sita' as a predicate.
Predicate vs function.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Predicate yields truth value; function yields object.

ai-c2-t15.quickRevision: A predicate is a relation or property symbol applied to a fixed number of arguments (terms); the number of arguments is its arity. Remember: Arity examples.

ai-c2-t16.title: ISA Hierarchy
ai-c2-t16.definition: The ISA hierarchy organises concepts using 'instance' and 'isa' links so that properties of general classes are inherited by their subclasses and individuals.
ai-c2-t16.simpleExplanation: ISA ka matlab 'is a'. Marcus ek man hai, man ek person hai, person ke properties neeche tak inherit hote hain. Isse knowledge repeat nahi likhni padti.
ai-c2-t16.realLifeAnalogy: Family tree of categories: Animal → Mammal → Dog → Tommy. Anything true for animals is automatically true for Tommy.
ai-c2-t16.example: instance(Marcus, Pompeian), isa(Pompeian, Roman), isa(Roman, Person). Property: Person has legs=2. Marcus inherits legs=2 through the chain.
keyPoints: instance: object ∈ class; isa: class ⊆ superclass.
Property inheritance goes up the hierarchy.
Reduces redundancy in the knowledge base.
Exceptions override defaults (penguin cannot fly).
Multiple inheritance may create conflicts.
Used in semantic nets, frames and ontologies.
commonMistakes: Using isa for an individual (should be instance).
Forgetting more specific information overrides inherited defaults.

examQuestions.question: Explain ISA hierarchy and inheritance.
examQuestions.answer: instance/isa links; properties inherited; exceptions override.

examQuestions.question: instance vs isa.
examQuestions.answer: instance links an individual to its class; isa links a subclass to its superclass.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is multiple inheritance?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A class inherits from more than one superclass.

knowledgeCheck.question: Bird can fly; Penguin isa Bird but cannot fly. What happens?
isa vs instance of.
knowledgeCheck.answer: isa is class-to-class; instance is object-to-class.

ai-c2-t16.quickRevision: The ISA hierarchy organises concepts using 'instance' and 'isa' links so that properties of general classes are inherited by their subclasses and individuals. Remember: Instance vs isa.

ai-c2-t17.title: Frame Notation
ai-c2-t17.definition: A frame is a data structure representing a stereotyped situation or object as slots (attributes) with values, defaults and attached procedures.
ai-c2-t17.simpleExplanation: Frame ek form ki tarah hai: slots (attributes) hote hain, unme values, default values aur kabhi kabhi procedures bhi. Frames ek doosre se isa/instance se jude hote hain.
ai-c2-t17.realLifeAnalogy: A registration form with fields: some fields are pre-filled with defaults, and the form for a Student inherits fields from the form for a Person.
ai-c2-t17.example: Frame Bird: legs=2, can_fly=yes(default). Frame Penguin: isa Bird, can_fly=no. Frame Tweety: instance Penguin. Query can_fly(Tweety) → no (Penguin overrides Bird).
keyPoints: Proposed by Marvin Minsky (1975).
Components: frame name, slots, fillers/values, facets.
Facets: value, default, range, if-needed, if-added, if-removed.
Inheritance through isa and instance slots.
Good for stereotypical knowledge and defaults.
Weak at complex logical reasoning; exceptions need care.
commonMistakes: Treating a frame as an object with methods exactly like OOP; it is a KR idea.
Forgetting inheritance of defaults.

examQuestions.question: Explain frames with example.
examQuestions.answer: Slots, fillers, defaults, inheritance; give Bird/Penguin/Tweety.

examQuestions.question: Frames vs semantic networks.
examQuestions.answer: Frames group all attributes of a concept in one structure with defaults/procedures; semantic nets use nodes and labelled arcs.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a slot?
knowledgeCheck.answer: An attribute of a frame that holds a value.

knowledgeCheck.question: Tweety (a penguin) can fly? using frames
knowledgeCheck.answer: No: the Penguin frame overrides the Bird default.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is an if-needed facet?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A procedure run to compute a value when it is requested.

ai-c2-t17.workedExample: Frame Car: wheels=4 (default), fuel=petrol. Frame ElectricCar: isa Car, fuel=electricity, wheels inherited=4. MyCar instance ElectricCar ⇒ wheels=4, fuel=electricity.
ai-c2-t17.quickRevision: A frame is a data structure representing a stereotyped situation or object as slots (attributes) with values, defaults and attached procedures. Remember: Slot, filler, facet terms.

ai-c2-t18.title: Resolution
ai-c2-t18.definition: Resolution is a refutation-based inference rule that proves a statement by adding its negation to the knowledge base (in clause form) and deriving the empty clause.
ai-c2-t18.simpleExplanation: Resolution me hum jo prove karna hai uska negation lete hain, sab ko clause form me convert karte hain, aur resolve karte jaate hain. Agar empty clause mil gaya to contradiction aaya, matlab original statement sach tha.
ai-c2-t18.realLifeAnalogy: Proof by contradiction in maths: assume the opposite, derive something impossible, so the original claim must be true.
ai-c2-t18.example: KB: P, P→Q, Q→R. Prove R. Clauses: P; ¬P∨Q; ¬Q∨R; negated goal ¬R. Resolve ¬R with ¬Q∨R → ¬Q. Resolve ¬Q with ¬P∨Q → ¬P. Resolve ¬P with P → empty clause ⇒ R proved.
keyPoints: Resolution rule: from (A∨B) and (¬A∨C) infer (B∨C).
Works on clauses (CNF).
Refutation: add ¬goal, derive empty clause.
Sound and refutation-complete.
Predicate logic needs conversion to clause form and unification.
Conversion: remove →, push ¬ in, standardise variables, Skolemise ∃, drop ∀, convert to CNF.
ifYouKnow: Explain why we negate the goal.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to negate the goal.
Resolving on more than one literal pair at a time.
Skipping standardising variables apart.

examQuestions.question: Explain resolution with algorithm.
examQuestions.answer: Convert KB to clauses, negate goal, resolve pairs until empty clause.

examQuestions.question: Prove R from P, P→Q, Q→R by resolution.
examQuestions.answer: Resolve ¬R with ¬Q∨R, then ¬P∨Q, then P ⇒ empty clause.

examQuestions.question: Unify P(x,f(y)) with P(a,f(b)).
examQuestions.answer: Substitution {x/a, y/b}.

examQuestions.question: Why is resolution called refutation procedure?
examQuestions.answer: It proves by refuting (contradicting) the negated goal.

knowledgeCheck.question: We add the negation of the goal.

algorithmSteps: 1. Convert all KB statements to clause form (CNF).
2. Negate the goal and convert it to clauses; add to KB.
3. Select two clauses with complementary literals (unify if predicate logic).
4. Add the resolvent to the clause set.
5. If the empty clause is derived → goal proved; if no new clauses → goal not provable.
6. Repeat steps 3–5.
ai-c2-t18.complexity: Worst case exponential in the number of clauses; strategies (unit preference, set of support) improve it.
ai-c2-t18.workedExample: Clauses: (1) P (2) ¬P∨Q (3) ¬Q∨R (4) ¬R. Resolve(3,4)=¬Q; Resolve(2,¬Q)=¬P; Resolve(1,¬P)=□ ⇒ R is proved.
ai-c2-t18.quickRevision: Resolution is a refutation-based inference rule that proves a statement by adding its negation to the knowledge base (in clause form) and deriving the empty clause. Remember: Clause-form steps.

ai-c2-t19.title: Natural Deduction
ai-c2-t19.definition: Natural deduction is a proof system with introduction and elimination rules for each logical connective, mirroring how people reason with assumptions.
ai-c2-t19.simpleExplanation: Natural deduction me hum insaan jaise proof likhte hain: assumption lo, rules apply karo aur assumption close (discharge) karke conclusion nikalo.
ai-c2-t19.realLifeAnalogy: Like writing a maths proof: 'assume P…, then Q…, therefore if P then Q'.
ai-c2-t19.example: Prove P→R from P→Q and Q→R. Assume P. By →E with P→Q get Q. By →E with Q→R get R. Discharge P by →I ⇒ P→R.
keyPoints: Each connective has introduction (I) and elimination (E) rules.
→E = Modus Ponens; →I discharges an assumption.
∧I, ∧E, ∨I, ∨E, ¬I, ¬E, ⊥ rules.
Proofs are trees/lists of lines with justifications.
More human-readable than resolution but harder to automate.
Sound and complete for first-order logic.
ifYouKnow: Name the rule for each line.
commonMistakes: Using an assumption after it was discharged.
Skipping justification of lines.

examQuestions.question: Explain natural deduction with an example.
examQuestions.answer: Rules with I/E; prove P→R from P→Q, Q→R using assumption P.

examQuestions.question: Natural deduction vs resolution.
examQuestions.answer: ND is human-style with assumptions and many rules; resolution is a single rule on clauses suited to machines.

knowledgeCheck.question: Natural deduction vs truth table.
knowledgeCheck.answer: ND derives conclusions by rules; truth table checks all interpretations.

algorithmSteps: 1. Write the premises.
2. Assume the antecedent of the goal implication.
3. Apply elimination/introduction rules to derive the consequent.
4. Discharge the assumption with →I to obtain the implication.
ai-c2-t19.workedExample: 1. P→Q (premise) 2. Q→R (premise) 3. P (assume) 4. Q (→E 1,3) 5. R (→E 2,4) 6. P→R (→I 3–5).
ai-c2-t19.quickRevision: Natural deduction is a proof system with introduction and elimination rules for each logical connective, mirroring how people reason with assumptions. Remember: Key rules: →I, →E, ∧I, ∧E.

ai-c3-t01.title: Representation and Mappings
ai-c3-t01.definition: Representation and mapping is the process of translating real-world facts into an internal formalism (forward mapping), reasoning there, and translating the results back (backward mapping).
ai-c3-t01.simpleExplanation: Real world ke facts ko computer ke symbols me badalna forward mapping hai. Symbols pe reasoning hoti hai. Result ko wapas English facts me badalna backward mapping hai. Dono mapping sahi honi chahiye, warna answer galat.
ai-c3-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Using a map app: real roads → map data (forward), route computed on the map, then turn-by-turn directions spoken back in words (backward).
ai-c3-t01.example: Fact: 'Spot is a dog.' → dog(Spot). Fact: 'Every dog has a tail.' → ∀x dog(x)→hastail(x). Reasoning gives hastail(Spot). Backward mapping: 'Spot has a tail.'
keyPoints: Two levels: facts (real world) and representation (symbols).
Forward mapping: facts → internal representation; backward mapping: representation → facts.
Reasoning programs work on the internal representation.
Mapping is generally not one-to-one: one fact may have many representations, and vice versa.
Operations on representations must correspond to valid operations on facts.
Knowledge level vs symbol level distinction.
ifYouKnow: Say why mapping errors give wrong answers.
commonMistakes: Thinking the representation is the knowledge itself; it only stands for facts.
Assuming mapping is always one-to-one.

examQuestions.question: Explain representation and mappings with a diagram.
examQuestions.answer: Facts → forward mapping → internal representation → reasoning → new representation → backward mapping → facts.

examQuestions.question: Is mapping between facts and representations one-to-one?
examQuestions.answer: No; many-to-many is common, which causes ambiguity.

knowledgeCheck.question: Reasoning is done on the real-world facts directly.
Why do we need backward mapping?
knowledgeCheck.answer: To express inferred results as facts humans understand.

knowledgeCheck.question: Two logic sentences encode the same English fact. What does it show?
What are the two levels in Rich & Knight's view?

ai-c3-t01.quickRevision: Facts →(forward map)→ representation → reason → representation →(backward map)→ facts. Mapping is not one-to-one.
ai-c3-t01.stateSpace: Facts ↔ symbols; operators work on symbol structures.

ai-c3-t02.title: Different Approaches to Knowledge Representation
ai-c3-t02.definition: The four approaches to knowledge representation are simple relational, inheritable, inferential and procedural knowledge.
ai-c3-t02.simpleExplanation: Knowledge ko 4 tareeke se rakh sakte hain: tables (relational), isa/inheritance se (inheritable), logic se (inferential), ya programs/rules se (procedural). Har ka alag kaam hai.
ai-c3-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Same cricket data can be stored as a score table, a class hierarchy (Player → Batter → Opener), logical rules ('if 3 wickets down then…') or coach's playbook steps.
ai-c3-t02.example: Players table (name, height, bats): relational. 'Pitcher isa Player; Player isa Person' with inherited attributes: inheritable. 'If bats right-handed and … then…': inferential. A scoring-procedure program: procedural.
keyPoints: Simple relational knowledge: facts in tables (databases); weak inference.
Inheritable knowledge: isa/instance hierarchies, slot-and-filler, inheritance.
Inferential knowledge: formal logic for deriving new facts.
Procedural knowledge: rules/programs saying how to do something.
Real systems mix approaches.
Each differs in inference power, efficiency and ease of update.
mustKnow: The four categories with an example each.
ifYouKnow: Name and distinguish the four approaches.
commonMistakes: Calling a database 'inferential'; simple relational tables can't derive new facts.
Treating procedural knowledge as just data.

examQuestions.question: Explain approaches to knowledge representation with examples.
examQuestions.answer: Relational, inheritable, inferential, procedural with a short example each.

examQuestions.question: Declarative vs procedural representation.
examQuestions.answer: Declarative stores facts and lets the system infer; procedural embeds how-to steps directly.

knowledgeCheck.question: Isa and instance links are used in:
Simple relational knowledge supports strong inference.

Relational vs inheritable.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Relational: flat tables; inheritable: class hierarchy with property inheritance.

ai-c3-t02.quickRevision: Four approaches: relational (tables), inheritable (isa), inferential (logic), procedural (rules/programs).

ai-c3-t03.title: Issues in Knowledge Representation
ai-c3-t03.definition: Issues in KR are the design questions about attributes, relationships among attributes, granularity, set representation and structure selection that decide how well a scheme works.
ai-c3-t03.simpleExplanation: KR banate waqt kuch sawal aate hain: kaunse attributes basic hain (isa, instance)? kitna detail rakhein? sets kaise rakhein? sahi structure kaise chunein? Inhi ko KR issues kehte hain.
ai-c3-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Designing a school database: which fields are universal (name, ID)? how detailed should addresses be? how to store groups of students? which table layout suits queries?
ai-c3-t03.example: Granularity: store 'John spotted Sue' as a single fact, or break into actions (see event, agent, object)? Fine-grained helps inference but costs more space/time.
keyPoints: Important attributes: instance and isa appear in almost every domain.
Relationships among attributes: inverses, existence in an isa hierarchy, techniques for reasoning about values, single-valued attributes.
Level of detail (granularity) of representation.
Representing sets of objects: classes vs instances, set-level properties.
Selecting the right structure at the right time.
Trade-off between expressiveness and efficiency.
ifYouKnow: Give an example of inverse attributes.
commonMistakes: Using too fine granularity for every problem.
Forgetting that single-valued attributes (e.g. height) need special handling.

examQuestions.question: Discuss the issues in knowledge representation.
examQuestions.answer: Important attributes, relationships among attributes, granularity, sets of objects, selecting the right structure.

examQuestions.question: What is granularity?
examQuestions.answer: The level of detail used to represent knowledge.

knowledgeCheck.question: Instance and isa are examples of:
Finer granularity always makes the system faster.
