knowledgeCheck.answer: An attribute with exactly one value for an object, e.g. height.

ai-c3-t03.quickRevision: Issues: key attributes, attribute relationships, granularity, sets, right structure.

ai-c3-t04.title: Predicate Logic
ai-c3-t04.definition: Predicate logic represents facts using predicates, functions, variables and quantifiers, and derives new facts using inference such as resolution.
ai-c3-t04.simpleExplanation: Predicate logic me facts ko predicates se likhte hain (man(Marcus)), isa/instance bhi logic me likh sakte hain, computable functions (jaise >) use kar sakte hain, aur resolution se answers prove karte hain.
ai-c3-t04.realLifeAnalogy: A rulebook with named relations: each sentence is precise, so a lawyer (the resolution procedure) can mechanically prove a claim.
ai-c3-t04.example: Facts: man(Marcus); Pompeian(Marcus); ∀x Pompeian(x)→Roman(x); ruler(Caesar); ∀x man(x)→person(x); tryassassinate(Marcus,Caesar); ∀x∀y person(x)∧ruler(y)∧tryassassinate(x,y)→¬loyalto(x,y). Prove ¬loyalto(Marcus,Caesar).
keyPoints: Simple facts: predicate(argument).
Instance and isa: instance(Marcus,man), isa(man,person); with axiom ∀x∀y∀z instance(x,y)∧isa(y,z)→instance(x,z).
Computable functions/predicates: gt(3,2), plus(2,3,5) evaluated by procedure, not stored as facts.
Resolution: convert to clauses, negate goal, resolve to empty clause.
Unification matches literals with substitutions.
Resolution is sound and refutation-complete.
commonMistakes: Storing all numeric comparisons as facts instead of computable predicates.
Missing the axiom that links instance and isa.

examQuestions.question: Prove ¬loyalto(Marcus,Caesar) by resolution.
examQuestions.answer: Negate goal: loyalto(Marcus,Caesar). Resolve with rule clause, ruler(Caesar), tryassassinate(Marcus,Caesar), man→person, man(Marcus) ⇒ empty clause.

examQuestions.question: Why use computable functions and predicates?
examQuestions.answer: Because infinitely many facts such as gt(5,3) cannot be stored; they are evaluated by procedures.

examQuestions.question: What is unification?
examQuestions.answer: Finding a substitution that makes two literals identical.

knowledgeCheck.question: Resolution proves a goal by:
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Derive empty clause from its negation.

knowledgeCheck.question: gt(5,3) should be stored as a fact in the KB.
Link instance(Marcus,man) and isa(man,person) to infer instance(Marcus,person).

ai-c3-t04.quickRevision: Predicate logic: facts as predicates, instance/isa axioms, computable predicates, resolution by refutation.
algorithmSteps: 1. Write facts as WFFs.
2. Convert to clause form; negate the goal.
3. Resolve pairs of clauses (with unification).
4. Stop when the empty clause is derived.
ai-c3-t04.workedExample: Clauses: ¬man(x)∨person(x); man(Marcus); ruler(Caesar); tryassassinate(Marcus,Caesar); ¬person(x)∨¬ruler(y)∨¬tryassassinate(x,y)∨¬loyalto(x,y); negated goal loyalto(Marcus,Caesar). Resolve goal with rule → ¬person(Marcus)∨¬ruler(Caesar)∨¬tryassassinate(Marcus,Caesar) → ¬person(Marcus)∨¬tryassassinate → ¬person(Marcus) → ¬man(Marcus) → □.

ai-c3-t05.title: Propositional Logic (Knowledge Representation)
ai-c3-t05.definition: In KR, propositional logic encodes facts as true/false propositions, infers using rules, and proves goals by resolution on clauses.
ai-c3-t05.simpleExplanation: Yahan propositional logic ko knowledge represent karne ke liye use karte hain: facts propositions hote hain, inference rules se naye facts nikalte hain, aur resolution se prove karte hain.
ai-c3-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A set of switches with wiring rules: you flip known switches (facts) and the rules decide which other lamps must be on.
ai-c3-t05.example: KB: R (it rains), R→W (rain makes ground wet), W→S (wet ground is slippery). Inference: MP gives W; MP gives S. Resolution check: clauses R, ¬R∨W, ¬W∨S, negated goal ¬S ⇒ empty clause.
keyPoints: Representation: atomic propositions + connectives.
Inference: model checking (truth table) or inference rules (MP, MT, HS).
Reasoning patterns: chaining implications (R→W→S), contraposition.
Resolution: CNF clauses, negate goal, derive empty clause.
Truth table inference is exponential: 2^n rows.
Horn clauses allow efficient forward/backward chaining.
commonMistakes: Writing 'all' statements as one proposition per object.
Confusing implication direction.

examQuestions.question: Show propositional representation, inference and resolution for Rain/Wet/Slippery.
examQuestions.answer: Facts R, R→W, W→S; derive S with MP twice; or resolution as above.

examQuestions.question: Why is truth-table inference costly?
examQuestions.answer: 2^n rows for n variables.

knowledgeCheck.question: Truth table with 4 variables has rows:
What is a Horn clause?
knowledgeCheck.answer: A clause with at most one positive literal.

knowledgeCheck.question: Truth-table vs resolution inference.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Truth table enumerates all models; resolution derives by clause manipulation.

ai-c3-t05.quickRevision: Propositional KR: facts as propositions, infer by MP/MT/HS, prove by resolution; truth tables cost 2^n.
algorithmSteps: 1. Encode facts and rules as propositional formulas.
2. Apply inference rules or convert to CNF.
3. Negate query and resolve to the empty clause.

ai-c3-t06.title: First-Order Logic
ai-c3-t06.definition: First-order logic (FOL) extends propositional logic with objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers, with inference via unification, generalized Modus Ponens and resolution.
ai-c3-t06.simpleExplanation: FOL me hum objects ke baare me general statements likh sakte hain (∀, ∃). Inference me instantiate karte hain (universal instantiation), chaining use karte hain ya resolution lagate hain.
ai-c3-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Propositional logic is a list of yes/no cards; FOL is a database with query language: it talks about every row and some rows.
ai-c3-t06.example: KB: ∀x King(x)∧Greedy(x)→Evil(x); King(John); Greedy(John). Universal instantiation x/John gives King(John)∧Greedy(John)→Evil(John). Modus Ponens ⇒ Evil(John).
keyPoints: Representation: constants, variables, predicates, functions, ∀, ∃.
Inference rules: universal instantiation, existential generalisation, existential instantiation (Skolem), generalized Modus Ponens.
Reasoning patterns: forward chaining (data-driven), backward chaining (goal-driven).
Resolution: CNF with Skolemisation and unification; refutation-complete.
FOL entailment is semi-decidable.
Horn-clause FOL supports efficient chaining (Prolog).
ifYouKnow: Run chaining on a small KB.
Explain why FOL is more expressive.
commonMistakes: Using the same Skolem constant for different existentials.
Applying UI to ∃ statements.

examQuestions.question: Explain representation, inference, reasoning patterns and resolution in FOL.
examQuestions.answer: Syntax with quantifiers; UI/EG/GMP; forward/backward chaining; resolution with unification.

examQuestions.question: From ∀x King(x)∧Greedy(x)→Evil(x), King(John), Greedy(John) derive Evil(John).
examQuestions.answer: UI x/John then MP.

examQuestions.question: What is Skolemisation?
examQuestions.answer: Replacing existential variables with Skolem constants/functions to eliminate ∃.

knowledgeCheck.question: ∃x P(x) after Skolemisation becomes:
knowledgeCheck.answer: P(c) for a new constant c
options: P(c) for a new constant c

knowledgeCheck.question: FOL is more expressive than propositional logic.
Forward vs backward chaining.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Forward starts with facts; backward starts with the goal.

ai-c3-t06.quickRevision: FOL = objects + predicates + quantifiers; inference by UI/GMP, chaining or resolution; Skolemise ∃.
algorithmSteps: 1. Represent KB in FOL.
2. Instantiate quantified rules (UI) or use unification.
3. Apply GMP / chaining, or convert to CNF, Skolemise, resolve with unification.
4. Stop when goal derived or empty clause obtained.
ai-c3-t06.workedExample: ∀x King(x)∧Greedy(x)→Evil(x); King(John); Greedy(John). θ={x/John}. GMP ⇒ Evil(John).

ai-c4-t01.title: Non-Monotonic Reasoning
ai-c4-t01.definition: Non-monotonic reasoning allows conclusions to be withdrawn when new information arrives, unlike monotonic reasoning where adding facts never removes conclusions.
ai-c4-t01.simpleExplanation: Classical logic me naya fact aane se purane conclusions delete nahi hote. Real life me hote hain: 'Tweety bird hai, to udta hai' — par agar pata chale Tweety penguin hai to conclusion wapas lena padta hai.
ai-c4-t01.realLifeAnalogy: You assume a shop is open at 10 am; when you see the shutter down you withdraw that assumption.
ai-c4-t01.example: Bird(Tweety) ⇒ assume Flies(Tweety). New fact Penguin(Tweety) ⇒ retract Flies(Tweety). Conclusion set shrank after adding knowledge.
keyPoints: Monotonic: KB ⊆ KB' ⇒ Conclusions(KB) ⊆ Conclusions(KB').
Non-monotonic: new knowledge can invalidate earlier conclusions.
Needed for incomplete information, defaults and changing worlds.
Techniques: default reasoning, circumscription, closed-world assumption, truth maintenance.
Conclusions are tentative (defeasible).
Abduction and belief revision are related.
ifYouKnow: Explain why classical logic is monotonic.
commonMistakes: Believing real-world reasoning is monotonic.
Confusing non-monotonic with uncertain probabilities.

examQuestions.question: Monotonic vs non-monotonic reasoning.
examQuestions.answer: Monotonic never loses conclusions with new facts; non-monotonic can.

examQuestions.question: Explain with Tweety.
examQuestions.answer: Default: birds fly; Tweety is a bird ⇒ flies; learning Tweety is a penguin retracts it.

knowledgeCheck.question: In non-monotonic reasoning new facts can:
Why needed?
knowledgeCheck.answer: To handle incomplete information and defaults.

knowledgeCheck.question: You assume a train is on time, then see a delay board. Reasoning type?
Monotonic vs non-monotonic.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Monotonic: conclusions only grow; non-monotonic: may shrink.

ai-c4-t01.quickRevision: Non-monotonic: conclusions can be withdrawn by new info (defaults); classical logic is monotonic.

ai-c4-t02.title: Logics for Non-Monotonic Reasoning
ai-c4-t02.definition: Non-monotonic logics are formal systems such as default logic, circumscription, closed-world assumption and modal (autoepistemic) logic that support defeasible conclusions.
ai-c4-t02.simpleExplanation: Non-monotonic reasoning ko formal banane ke liye kuch logics hain: default logic, circumscription, closed-world assumption aur modal logic. Sab ka maqsad hai 'jab tak galat sabit na ho, ye maan lo'.
ai-c4-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Legal system: a person is presumed innocent (default) unless evidence proves otherwise.
ai-c4-t02.example: Default rule: bird(x) : flies(x) / flies(x) — if x is a bird and it is consistent to assume x flies, conclude x flies. Modal form: ∀x bird(x) ∧ M flies(x) → flies(x), where M means 'is consistent'.
keyPoints: Default logic (Reiter): rule A:B/C = if A holds and B is consistent, conclude C.
Modal (autoepistemic) logic: M operator = 'consistent with beliefs'.
Circumscription: minimise the extension of abnormal predicates.
Closed-world assumption (CWA): anything not provably true is false (Prolog negation as failure).
Problems: computing consistency is hard/undecidable; multiple extensions.
Used in diagnosis and planning.
commonMistakes: Applying CWA where information is genuinely missing (not false).
Forgetting a default is overridden by contrary evidence.

examQuestions.question: Explain logics for non-monotonic reasoning.
examQuestions.answer: Default logic, modal logic with M, circumscription and CWA with examples.

examQuestions.question: Open-world vs closed-world assumption.
examQuestions.answer: OWA: unknown ≠ false; CWA: unprovable ⇒ false.

knowledgeCheck.question: Default logic rule A:B/C needs B to be consistent.
What does M mean in modal non-monotonic logic?
A database says a flight is not listed; so assume it is cancelled. Assumption?
Circumscription vs default logic.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Circumscription minimises abnormal things; default logic applies rules while consistent.

ai-c4-t02.quickRevision: Logics: default (A:B/C), modal M, circumscription, CWA. All allow retractable conclusions.

ai-c4-t03.title: Forward Rules and Backward Rules
ai-c4-t03.definition: Forward rules (forward chaining) reason from known facts to conclusions; backward rules (backward chaining) reason from a goal back to supporting facts.
ai-c4-t03.simpleExplanation: Forward chaining: facts se shuru karke naye facts nikalte jao (data-driven). Backward chaining: goal se shuru karke dekho kya prove karna padega (goal-driven).
ai-c4-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Forward: cooking with whatever ingredients you have to see what dishes you can make. Backward: choosing a dish first, then checking if the ingredients are available.
ai-c4-t03.example: Rules: R1 A∧B→C; R2 C→D; R3 D∧E→F. Facts: A, B, E. Forward: C, then D, then F. Backward goal F: need D and E; E is a fact; D needs C; C needs A and B ✓ ⇒ F proved.
keyPoints: Forward chaining is data-driven; backward chaining is goal-driven.
Forward may derive many irrelevant facts; backward explores only relevant ones.
Backward chaining is used in Prolog and diagnostic systems (MYCIN).
Forward is good for monitoring/configuration (XCON).
Both are sound; complete for Horn clauses.
Conflict resolution decides which rule to fire first.
mustKnow: Two algorithms and the A,B,E example.
ifYouKnow: Run both chainings on a KB.
Choose a method for a task.
commonMistakes: Mixing up direction: forward starts from facts.
Ignoring conflict resolution.

examQuestions.question: Forward vs backward chaining.
examQuestions.answer: Facts→goal vs goal→facts; data-driven vs goal-driven; use cases.

examQuestions.question: Apply both methods to R1–R3 with facts A,B,E.
examQuestions.answer: Forward: C,D,F. Backward: F ⇐ D,E ⇐ C ⇐ A,B.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where is backward chaining best?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Diagnosis, where a specific hypothesis is tested.

knowledgeCheck.question: Facts P; rules P→Q, Q→R. Forward result?

algorithmSteps: Forward: 1. Put known facts in working memory.
2. Find rules whose conditions match.
3. Fire one (conflict resolution); add conclusion.
4. Repeat until goal found or no rule fires.
Backward: 1. Take goal G.
2. If G is a fact → success.
3. Else find a rule concluding G; make its conditions sub-goals.
4. Recurse; fail if none works.

ai-c4-t04.title: Justification-Based Truth Maintenance Systems
ai-c4-t04.definition: A Justification-based Truth Maintenance System (JTMS) records why each belief is held (its justifications) and updates beliefs as assumptions change.
ai-c4-t04.simpleExplanation: JTMS har belief ke saath uski 'wajah' (justification) yaad rakhta hai. Wajah badli to belief IN (maana hua) ya OUT (nahi maana) ho jata hai, aur dependent beliefs apne aap update ho jaate hain.
ai-c4-t04.realLifeAnalogy: A spreadsheet: change one cell and all cells that depend on it update. JTMS does this for beliefs.
ai-c4-t04.example: Node A: Bird(Tweety) IN (premise). Node B: Flies(Tweety) justified by SL (A)(Abnormal) — IN if A is IN and Abnormal is OUT. Add Penguin(Tweety) ⇒ Abnormal IN ⇒ B becomes OUT automatically.
keyPoints: Nodes have status IN (believed) or OUT (not believed).
Justification: support list SL (in-list)(out-list); node is IN if all in-list nodes IN and all out-list nodes OUT.
Premises always IN; assumptions are retractable.
Contradiction nodes trigger dependency-directed backtracking.
Maintains consistency and avoids recomputation.
Complement: ATMS (assumption-based) keeps multiple contexts.
commonMistakes: Thinking JTMS performs inference; it only maintains beliefs.
Confusing IN with 'true'; IN means currently believed.

examQuestions.question: Explain JTMS with an example.
examQuestions.answer: Nodes, justifications, IN/OUT labels; Tweety flies example.

examQuestions.question: What is dependency-directed backtracking?
examQuestions.answer: On contradiction, backtrack only to the assumptions that caused it.

knowledgeCheck.question: Abnormal(Tweety) becomes IN. What happens to Flies(Tweety)?
JTMS vs ATMS?
knowledgeCheck.answer: JTMS keeps one consistent context; ATMS tracks many assumption sets.

ai-c4-t04.quickRevision: JTMS: nodes IN/OUT, SL justifications, dependency-directed backtracking keep beliefs consistent.
algorithmSteps: 1. Add nodes with justifications (SL in-list, out-list).
2. Label a node IN if its justification is satisfied; else OUT.
3. When a node changes status, propagate to dependants.
4. If a contradiction node is IN, find responsible assumptions and retract one.

ai-c4-t05.title: Semantic Nets
ai-c4-t05.definition: A semantic net is a graph of nodes (concepts/objects) connected by labelled arcs (relations) used to represent knowledge and support inheritance.
ai-c4-t05.simpleExplanation: Semantic net ek graph hai: nodes = concepts, arrows = relations (isa, instance, has-part). Isse inheritance se naye facts mil jaate hain.
ai-c4-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A mind map: the central idea connects to branches with labelled links.
ai-c4-t05.example: Tom –instance→ Cat –isa→ Mammal –has→ Fur. Query 'Does Tom have fur?' → follow instance and isa arcs ⇒ yes by inheritance.
keyPoints: Nodes = objects/classes; arcs = labelled relations.
Standard links: isa (class–class), instance (object–class).
Property inheritance by following isa/instance upward.
Answer queries by intersection search (spreading activation).
Partitioned nets represent quantification.
Limitations: no formal semantics, hard to represent negation/quantifiers.
commonMistakes: Mixing isa and instance arcs.
Assuming semantic nets have the precise semantics of logic.

examQuestions.question: Explain semantic networks with example.
examQuestions.answer: Nodes, arcs, isa/instance, inheritance, Tom example.

examQuestions.question: Drawback of semantic nets?
examQuestions.answer: No standard semantics; weak at quantifiers and negation.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does an instance arc connect?
Tom is a cat, cats are mammals. Is Tom a mammal?
Semantic net vs frame.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Nets are graphs; frames bundle slots/defaults.

ai-c4-t05.quickRevision: Semantic net = nodes + labelled arcs; isa/instance inheritance; weak semantics.

ai-c4-t06.title: Statistical Reasoning
ai-c4-t06.definition: Statistical reasoning handles uncertainty by assigning numeric degrees of belief such as probabilities or certainty factors to statements.
ai-c4-t06.simpleExplanation: Jab pakka sach/jhooth nahi pata, to numbers (probability, certainty factor) se belief represent karte hain aur unhe combine karke conclusion nikalte hain.
ai-c4-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Weather forecast: '70% chance of rain' is a number-based belief that helps you decide about an umbrella.
ai-c4-t06.example: MYCIN certainty factors: rule 1 supports hypothesis with CF 0.6 and rule 2 with CF 0.5. Combined CF = 0.6 + 0.5×(1−0.6) = 0.8.
keyPoints: Probability: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1; P(A|B)=P(A∧B)/P(B).
Certainty factor CF = MB − MD (measure of belief minus disbelief), range −1…+1.
Combining two positive CFs: CF1 + CF2(1−CF1).
Dempster–Shafer theory models ignorance with belief intervals.
Fuzzy logic handles vagueness, not randomness.
Bayesian methods use prior knowledge and evidence.
commonMistakes: Treating CF as true probability; it is an ad-hoc measure.
Mixing vagueness (fuzzy) with uncertainty (probability).

examQuestions.question: Explain approaches to statistical reasoning.
examQuestions.answer: Probability/Bayes, certainty factors, Dempster–Shafer, fuzzy logic.

knowledgeCheck.question: Fuzzy vs probability.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Fuzzy = degree of truth; probability = chance of an event.

ai-c4-t06.quickRevision: Statistical reasoning: probability, CF (MB−MD), combine CF1+CF2(1−CF1), Dempster–Shafer.

ai-c4-t07.title: Probability and Bayes' Theorem
ai-c4-t07.definition: Bayes' theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis H after seeing evidence E: P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E).
ai-c4-t07.simpleExplanation: Bayes theorem batata hai evidence milne ke baad hypothesis ki probability kaise badalti hai. Prior belief + likelihood se posterior milta hai.
ai-c4-t07.realLifeAnalogy: A doctor's suspicion: before the test you suspect a rare disease slightly; a positive test raises that suspicion, but not to certainty.
keyPoints: Prior P(H); likelihood P(E|H); posterior P(H|E).
P(E)=Σ P(E|Hi)P(Hi) (total probability).
Bayes: P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E).
Independence: P(A∧B)=P(A)P(B).
Naive Bayes assumes features independent given class.
Base-rate neglect: ignoring the prior misleads.
commonMistakes: Confusing P(E|H) with P(H|E).
Forgetting to compute P(E) via total probability.

examQuestions.question: State Bayes' theorem.
examQuestions.answer: P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E).

examQuestions.question: What is base-rate neglect?
examQuestions.answer: Ignoring prior probability when interpreting evidence.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Bayes' theorem P(H) is called:
Prior vs posterior.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Prior: belief before evidence; posterior: after evidence.

ai-c4-t07.quickRevision: Bayes: P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E). Prior→posterior. Don't ignore base rates.
algorithmSteps: 1. Identify H and E; choose prior P(H).
2. Get likelihoods P(E|H) and P(E|¬H).
3. Compute P(E)=P(E|H)P(H)+P(E|¬H)P(¬H).
4. Compute posterior P(H|E).

ai-c4-t08.title: Bayesian Network
ai-c4-t08.definition: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are random variables with conditional probability tables, giving a compact joint distribution.
ai-c4-t08.simpleExplanation: Bayesian network ek DAG hai: har node ek variable, arrows direct influence dikhate hain, aur har node ke paas CPT hota hai. Isse bada joint probability table chhote tables me toot jaata hai.
ai-c4-t08.realLifeAnalogy: A family tree of causes: rain causes wet grass; each node only remembers how its parents affect it.
keyPoints: Structure: DAG; nodes = variables; edges = direct dependence.
CPT: P(Xi | Parents(Xi)).
Joint: P(X1…Xn)=∏ P(Xi|Parents(Xi)).
Conditional independence: a node is independent of non-descendants given its parents.
Inference: enumeration, variable elimination, approximate sampling.
Used in diagnosis, spam filtering, risk analysis.
commonMistakes: Using a graph with cycles.
Reading arrows as certain causation instead of probabilistic dependence.

examQuestions.question: Explain Bayesian networks.
examQuestions.answer: DAG + CPTs, joint factorisation, independence, inference.

examQuestions.question: Why is a BN compact?
examQuestions.answer: It stores local CPTs instead of the full joint table (2^n entries).

knowledgeCheck.question: What is stored at each node?
BN vs Markov network.
knowledgeCheck.answer: BN is directed with CPTs; Markov network is undirected with potentials.

ai-c4-t08.quickRevision: BN: DAG + CPTs; P(joint)=∏P(Xi|parents); compact; infer by enumeration/elimination.
algorithmSteps: 1. Identify variables and dependencies; draw DAG.
2. Specify a CPT for each node.
3. Write the query and evidence.
4. Sum out hidden variables (enumeration/elimination); normalise.

ai-c4-t09.title: Markov Networks
ai-c4-t09.definition: A Markov network (Markov random field) is an undirected graphical model whose joint distribution is a normalised product of potential functions over cliques.
ai-c4-t09.simpleExplanation: Markov network undirected graph hota hai. Edges sirf 'related hain' batate hain, direction nahi. Joint probability cliques ke potentials ke product se banti hai aur Z se normalise hoti hai.
ai-c4-t09.realLifeAnalogy: A friendship graph: neighbours tend to like similar things, but no one 'causes' another.
ai-c4-t09.example: Chain A–B–C: P(A,B,C)=(1/Z)φ1(A,B)φ2(B,C). A and C are independent given B (B separates them).
keyPoints: Undirected graph; nodes = variables.
Joint P(x)=(1/Z)∏ φ_C(x_C) over cliques C.
Z = partition function (normaliser).
Markov property: a node is independent of others given its neighbours.
Suits symmetric dependencies (images, social networks).
Computing Z is expensive.
ifYouKnow: Write the joint for a small graph.
commonMistakes: Treating potentials as probabilities (they need normalising).
Confusing a Markov chain with a Markov network.

examQuestions.question: Explain Markov networks.
examQuestions.answer: Undirected graph, clique potentials, partition function, Markov property.

examQuestions.question: Bayesian vs Markov network.
examQuestions.answer: Directed CPTs/no normalisation vs undirected potentials with Z.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is Z?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Partition function that normalises the product of potentials.

knowledgeCheck.question: A–B–C chain: given B, A and C are…
Markov chain vs Markov network.
knowledgeCheck.answer: A Markov chain models sequences over time; a Markov network models dependencies among variables in an undirected graph.

ai-c4-t09.quickRevision: Markov network: undirected, P=(1/Z)∏φ(cliques), Z normalises, node ⊥ rest | neighbours.

ai-c4-t10.title: Hidden Markov Model
ai-c4-t10.definition: A Hidden Markov Model (HMM) models a system whose states are hidden but produce observable outputs, defined by initial, transition and emission probabilities.
ai-c4-t10.simpleExplanation: HMM me asli state chhupi hoti hai (jaise mausam), hum sirf observations dekhte hain (jaise aap kya kar rahe ho). Observations se hidden states ka andaza lagate hain.
ai-c4-t10.realLifeAnalogy: Guessing the weather outside from whether your friend carries an umbrella or sunglasses.
ai-c4-t10.example: States: Rainy, Sunny. π: R 0.6, S 0.4. A: R→R 0.7, R→S 0.3, S→R 0.4, S→S 0.6. B: R: walk 0.1, shop 0.4, clean 0.5; S: walk 0.6, shop 0.3, clean 0.1. P(walk, shop)=α2(R)+α2(S)=0.0552+0.0486=0.1038.
keyPoints: Parameters λ=(A,B,π): transition, emission, initial.
Markov assumption: next state depends only on the current state.
Output independence: observation depends only on the current state.
Three problems: evaluation (forward algorithm), decoding (Viterbi), learning (Baum–Welch).
Forward/Viterbi complexity O(N²T).
Used in speech recognition, POS tagging, bioinformatics.
commonMistakes: Confusing hidden states with observations.
Using Viterbi for evaluation (it is for decoding).

examQuestions.question: Explain HMM and its three problems.
examQuestions.answer: Evaluation: forward; decoding: Viterbi; learning: Baum–Welch.

examQuestions.question: State the Markov assumption.
examQuestions.answer: Next state depends only on the present state.

knowledgeCheck.question: In HMM the states are directly observed.
What is the emission probability?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Probability of an observation given a state.

knowledgeCheck.question: Forward vs Viterbi.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Forward sums over all paths (probability); Viterbi picks the single best path.

ai-c4-t10.quickRevision: HMM: hidden states, observations, λ=(A,B,π); forward (evaluate), Viterbi (decode), Baum–Welch (learn).
algorithmSteps: Forward: 1. α1(i)=π_i·B_i(o1).
2. αt+1(j)=[Σ αt(i)·A_ij]·B_j(o_t+1).
3. P(O)=Σ αT(i).
ai-c4-t10.complexity: Forward and Viterbi: O(N²T) time, O(NT) space.

ai-c4-t11.title: Basis of Utility Theory
ai-c4-t11.definition: Utility theory says a rational agent should choose the action with maximum expected utility, where preferences over outcomes satisfy consistency axioms.
ai-c4-t11.simpleExplanation: Rational agent wo action chunta hai jisse uski expected utility sabse zyada ho. Utility = outcome kitna pasand hai uska number.
ai-c4-t11.realLifeAnalogy: Choosing between a sure ₹40 and a coin-flip for ₹100: you compare average satisfaction, not just the money.
ai-c4-t11.example: Gamble: 50% win 100, 50% win 0 ⇒ EU=50. Sure 40 ⇒ EU=40. A risk-neutral agent picks the gamble.
keyPoints: EU(a)=Σ P(s|a)·U(s).
Maximum Expected Utility (MEU) principle.
Preference axioms: orderability, transitivity, continuity, substitutability, monotonicity, decomposability.
Preferences over lotteries; U is unique up to positive linear transform.
Risk attitude shows in the shape of U.
Basis of decision-theoretic agents and decision networks.
commonMistakes: Maximising expected money instead of expected utility.
Violating transitivity of preferences.

examQuestions.question: EU of 50% ₹100 / 50% ₹0 vs sure ₹40.
examQuestions.answer: EU=50 so choose gamble if risk-neutral.

examQuestions.question: State the MEU principle.
examQuestions.answer: Choose the action maximising expected utility.

knowledgeCheck.question: Agent prefers A>B and B>C but C>A. Violated axiom?

ai-c4-t11.quickRevision: Utility theory: choose action with max EU=ΣP·U; preferences must be rational (transitive etc.).

ai-c4-t12.title: Utility Functions
ai-c4-t12.definition: A utility function maps each outcome to a real number expressing how desirable it is to the agent; its shape shows risk attitude.
ai-c4-t12.simpleExplanation: Utility function outcome ko number deta hai. Number ka curve batata hai agent risk-averse hai, risk-neutral ya risk-seeking.
ai-c4-t12.realLifeAnalogy: ₹100 matters a lot to a student but little to a millionaire: same money, different utility.
ai-c4-t12.example: U(x)=√x. Gamble: 50% ₹100, 50% ₹0 ⇒ EU=0.5·10=5. Sure ₹25 gives U=5 (certainty equivalent=25). So sure ₹40 (U≈6.3) is preferred: risk-averse.
keyPoints: U: outcomes → ℝ.
Risk-averse: concave U (diminishing returns).
Risk-neutral: linear U.
Risk-seeking: convex U.
Certainty equivalent: sure amount with the same utility as the gamble.
Multi-attribute utility combines several attributes (cost, time, safety).
commonMistakes: Equating utility with money.
Thinking all agents share the same U.

examQuestions.question: Risk-averse vs risk-seeking.
examQuestions.answer: Concave vs convex utility.

knowledgeCheck.question: Define certainty equivalent.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Sure amount equal in utility to the gamble.

ai-c4-t12.quickRevision: Utility function U(outcome)→ℝ; concave=risk-averse, linear=neutral, convex=seeking.
ai-c4-t12.workedExample: U=√x. Gamble (100,0)@50%: EU=5 → CE=25. A sure 40 (U=6.32) is better.

ai-c5-t01.title: Fuzzy Set Operations
ai-c5-t01.definition: Fuzzy set operations (union, intersection, complement) combine fuzzy sets whose elements have membership degrees between 0 and 1.
ai-c5-t01.simpleExplanation: Crisp set me element ya to hai ya nahi. Fuzzy set me element kitna belong karta hai (0 se 1) wo likhte hain. Union = max, intersection = min, complement = 1 − μ.
ai-c5-t01.realLifeAnalogy: 'Tall' is not yes/no: 5'6" is a little tall, 6'2" is very tall. Fuzzy sets capture that gradual boundary.
keyPoints: Membership μ_A(x) ∈ [0,1].
Union: μ=max(μA,μB). Intersection: μ=min(μA,μB). Complement: 1−μA.
Other forms: algebraic sum/product, bounded sum.
Support: μ>0; core: μ=1; height: max μ; α-cut: {x: μ≥α}.
A∪A′ ≠ universe and A∩A′ ≠ ∅ in general (excluded middle fails).
Reduces to crisp operations when μ ∈ {0,1}.
ifYouKnow: Explain how it differs from crisp sets.
commonMistakes: Using sum instead of max for union.
Assuming A∩A′=∅ for fuzzy sets.

examQuestions.question: Compute A∪B, A∩B, A′ for the given sets.
examQuestions.answer: As above.

examQuestions.question: Is the law of excluded middle valid for fuzzy sets?
examQuestions.answer: No; A∪A′ need not be the universe.

knowledgeCheck.question: Define α-cut.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Set of elements with μ ≥ α.

algorithmSteps: 1. For each element read μA(x), μB(x).
2. Union: take max; intersection: min; complement: 1−μ.
3. Write the resulting set.

ai-c5-t02.title: Membership Functions
ai-c5-t02.definition: A membership function maps each element of the universe of discourse to a degree of membership in [0,1] for a fuzzy set.
ai-c5-t02.simpleExplanation: Membership function batata hai kisi value ka fuzzy set me kitna hissa hai. Common shapes: triangle, trapezoid, Gaussian.
ai-c5-t02.realLifeAnalogy: A thermometer scale that says what temperature feels 'warm': 20° is half warm, 25° fully warm.
keyPoints: Triangular (a,b,c): rises a→b, falls b→c.
Trapezoidal (a,b,c,d): flat top between b and c.
Gaussian: exp(−(x−m)²/2σ²).
Chosen from expert knowledge or data.
Fuzzification: crisp input → membership values.
Shape affects system smoothness.
ifYouKnow: Compute μ for a triangular MF.
commonMistakes: Using MF outside range gives >1 or <0.
Confusing MF with a probability density.

examQuestions.question: Types of membership functions.
examQuestions.answer: Triangular, trapezoidal, Gaussian, sigmoid.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which MF has a flat top?
What is fuzzification?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Converting a crisp input into membership degrees.

knowledgeCheck.question: MF vs probability density.
knowledgeCheck.answer: MF measures degree of belonging; density measures likelihood.

ai-c5-t02.quickRevision: MF maps x→[0,1]; triangle/trapezoid/Gaussian; fuzzification = crisp→μ.

ai-c5-t03.title: Fuzzy Logic
ai-c5-t03.definition: Fuzzy logic is a many-valued logic where truth values range continuously between 0 and 1, allowing reasoning with vague concepts.
ai-c5-t03.simpleExplanation: Boolean logic me sach ya jhooth. Fuzzy logic me 'thoda sach' bhi hota hai. 'Temperature is high' 0.7 sach ho sakta hai.
ai-c5-t03.realLifeAnalogy: A dimmer switch instead of an on/off switch.
ai-c5-t03.example: Truth(temperature is high)=0.7, Truth(humidity is high)=0.4. AND=min=0.4; OR=max=0.7; NOT(temp high)=0.3.
keyPoints: Introduced by Lotfi Zadeh (1965).
Operators: AND=min, OR=max, NOT=1−x.
Linguistic variables: e.g. temperature ∈ {cold, warm, hot}.
Handles vagueness, not randomness.
Applications: washing machines, ACs, cameras, control systems.
Fuzzy ≠ probability.
commonMistakes: Treating 0.7 as a 70% chance; it is a degree of truth.
Calling fuzzy logic 'approximate probability'.

examQuestions.question: Fuzzy logic vs Boolean logic.
examQuestions.answer: Boolean: {0,1}; fuzzy: [0,1].

examQuestions.question: Who introduced fuzzy sets?
examQuestions.answer: Lotfi Zadeh, 1965.

knowledgeCheck.question: Fuzzy vs probability.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Fuzzy = degree of truth/vagueness; probability = likelihood/uncertainty.

ai-c5-t03.quickRevision: Fuzzy logic: truth in [0,1]; AND=min, OR=max, NOT=1−x; handles vagueness (Zadeh).

ai-c5-t04.title: Hedges
ai-c5-t04.definition: Hedges are linguistic modifiers such as very, somewhat or not that change the membership function of a fuzzy set.
ai-c5-t04.simpleExplanation: Hedge ek word hai jo fuzzy meaning ko badal deta hai: 'very tall' kam logon ko tall maanega, 'somewhat tall' zyada logon ko.
ai-c5-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Adjusting the strictness of an examiner: 'very strict' lowers pass chances, 'fairly lenient' raises them.
ai-c5-t04.example: μ_tall(Ravi)=0.64. very tall=0.64²=0.4096. somewhat tall=√0.64=0.8. not tall=1−0.64=0.36.
keyPoints: very: μ²   (concentration).
extremely: μ³.
somewhat/more or less: √μ   (dilation).
slightly: μ^1.7 approx.
not: 1−μ.
Hedges let rules be written in natural language.
ifYouKnow: Apply hedges to a membership value.
commonMistakes: Using square root for 'very'.
Forgetting hedges can be stacked ('very very').

examQuestions.question: What is dilation?
examQuestions.answer: Hedge that increases membership (e.g. √μ).

knowledgeCheck.question: Concentration vs dilation.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Concentration lowers μ (very); dilation raises μ (somewhat).

ai-c5-t05.title: Fuzzy Proposition and Inference Rules
ai-c5-t05.definition: A fuzzy proposition has a truth degree in [0,1]; fuzzy inference rules (IF–THEN with generalized Modus Ponens) derive conclusions from fuzzy premises.
ai-c5-t05.simpleExplanation: Fuzzy proposition: 'x is A' jiska truth degree hota hai. Fuzzy IF-THEN rule ('IF temp is high THEN fan is fast') me input ka degree batata hai output kitna activate hoga.
ai-c5-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A recipe: 'if the soup is a bit salty, add a little water': the amount depends on how salty it is.
ai-c5-t05.example: Rule: IF temperature is high THEN fan speed is fast. If μ_high(35°C)=0.7, the rule fires with strength 0.7; Mamdani min clips the 'fast' output set at 0.7.
keyPoints: Fuzzy proposition: 'x is A', truth=μA(x).
Rule: IF x is A THEN y is B.
Generalised Modus Ponens: rule A→B and fact x is A′ ⇒ y is B′.
Compositional rule of inference: B′=A′∘R.
Mamdani implication: min(μA,μB); Larsen: product.
Multiple rules combine outputs by max (aggregation).
commonMistakes: Treating fuzzy rules as crisp triggers.
Forgetting aggregation across rules.

examQuestions.question: Explain fuzzy propositions and inference.
examQuestions.answer: Propositions, IF-THEN rules, GMP, min/product implication.

examQuestions.question: μ_high(35)=0.7 under Mamdani: output set?
examQuestions.answer: 'Fast' clipped at 0.7.

knowledgeCheck.question: State GMP.
knowledgeCheck.answer: From A→B and A′ infer B′.

knowledgeCheck.question: Rule antecedents μ=0.6 AND μ=0.8. Firing strength?
Mamdani vs Larsen.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Mamdani clips with min; Larsen scales with product.

ai-c5-t05.quickRevision: Fuzzy rule IF A THEN B: firing=antecedent degree; Mamdani min clip; aggregate with max; GMP.
algorithmSteps: 1. Fuzzify inputs to get μ values.
2. Firing strength = min (AND) of antecedents.
3. Clip/scale each rule's output set.
4. Aggregate outputs with max.

ai-c5-t06.title: Fuzzy Systems
ai-c5-t06.definition: A fuzzy system uses fuzzification, a fuzzy rule base, an inference engine and defuzzification to map crisp inputs to crisp outputs.
ai-c5-t06.simpleExplanation: Fuzzy system crisp input leta hai, usse fuzzy banata hai, rules lagata hai aur fir wapas crisp output deta hai (defuzzification). Washing machine isi tarah load ke hisaab se time decide karti hai.
ai-c5-t06.realLifeAnalogy: A skilled chef: reads 'a bit hot' from the stove, applies kitchen rules, and finally picks an exact knob setting.
ai-c5-t06.example: Fan controller: input temperature 32°C → fuzzify (hot 0.6) → rule: IF hot THEN speed fast → aggregate → defuzzify to e.g. 74 rpm. Sugeno: rules w=0.6 (z=20) and w=0.4 (z=80) ⇒ z=(0.6·20+0.4·80)/1.0=44.
keyPoints: Blocks: fuzzifier → rule base + inference engine → defuzzifier.
Mamdani: fuzzy outputs; Sugeno (TSK): crisp linear/constant outputs.
Defuzzification: centroid (centre of gravity), mean of maxima, weighted average.
Knowledge from experts in IF–THEN form.
Robust to noise; no precise mathematical model needed.
Applications: ACs, washing machines, ABS, cameras.
commonMistakes: Skipping defuzzification.
Mixing Sugeno's crisp outputs with Mamdani's fuzzy outputs.

examQuestions.question: Explain architecture of a fuzzy system.
examQuestions.answer: Fuzzifier, knowledge base/rules, inference engine, defuzzifier.

examQuestions.question: Mamdani vs Sugeno.
examQuestions.answer: Mamdani has fuzzy consequents needing defuzzification; Sugeno has crisp functions with weighted average.

knowledgeCheck.question: Order of blocks?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Fuzzifier, inference engine with rules, defuzzifier.

knowledgeCheck.question: A washing machine decides wash time from load and dirt using rules. System type?

ai-c5-t06.quickRevision: Fuzzy system: fuzzify → rules/inference → defuzzify (centroid/weighted avg); Mamdani vs Sugeno.
algorithmSteps: 1. Fuzzify crisp inputs.
2. Evaluate rules → firing strengths.
3. Aggregate outputs.
4. Defuzzify to crisp output.

ai-c6-t01.title: Introduction to Natural Language Processing
ai-c6-t01.definition: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the area of AI that enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language.
ai-c6-t01.simpleExplanation: Computer ko insaan ki bhasha (Hindi, English) samjhana aur bolna NLP hai. Ye mushkil hai kyunki language me ambiguity hoti hai.
ai-c6-t01.realLifeAnalogy: A translator who must understand words, grammar, meaning and context before replying.
ai-c6-t01.example: Chatbot: user types 'book a table for two at 8'. NLP extracts intent=book_table, party=2, time=8pm and replies.
keyPoints: NLU (understanding) and NLG (generation).
Levels of analysis: phonological, morphological, lexical, syntactic, semantic, discourse, pragmatic.
Challenges: ambiguity (lexical, syntactic, semantic), context, idioms.
Applications: machine translation, chatbots, summarisation, sentiment analysis, speech interfaces.
Typical pipeline: tokenisation → tagging → parsing → semantics → pragmatics.
Approaches: rule-based, statistical, neural.
commonMistakes: Treating NLP as keyword matching.
Forgetting pragmatics (context).

examQuestions.question: Explain NLP and its levels.
examQuestions.answer: Definition; NLU/NLG; the seven levels; applications.

examQuestions.question: Example of lexical ambiguity?
examQuestions.answer: 'Bank' = riverbank or financial bank.

knowledgeCheck.question: Pragmatics deals with context of use.
'I saw the man with a telescope' has two meanings. Ambiguity type?
NLU vs NLG.
knowledgeCheck.answer: NLU maps text to meaning; NLG maps meaning to text.

ai-c6-t01.quickRevision: NLP: NLU+NLG; levels morphological→syntactic→semantic→discourse→pragmatic; ambiguity is the core difficulty.

ai-c6-t02.title: Syntactic Processing
ai-c6-t02.definition: Syntactic processing (parsing) analyses a sentence's grammatical structure and builds a parse tree using a grammar.
ai-c6-t02.simpleExplanation: Syntactic processing sentence ka grammar structure nikalta hai: kaun subject, kaun verb, kaun object. Result ek parse tree hota hai.
ai-c6-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Like sentence diagramming in school grammar class.
ai-c6-t02.example: Grammar: S→NP VP; NP→Det N; VP→V NP. 'The cat chased a mouse': S[NP[The cat] VP[chased NP[a mouse]]].
keyPoints: Parsing uses a grammar (CFG) and a lexicon.
Top-down parsing starts from S; bottom-up from words.
Parse tree shows constituents.
Ambiguity gives multiple parse trees.
Parsers: recursive descent, chart parsing, CYK (O(n³)), ATN.
Output feeds semantic analysis.
commonMistakes: Thinking correct syntax means correct meaning ('Colorless green ideas sleep furiously').
Ignoring multiple parses.

examQuestions.question: Parse 'The cat chased a mouse'.
examQuestions.answer: S→NP VP; NP→Det N; VP→V NP; give tree.

examQuestions.question: Top-down vs bottom-up parsing.
examQuestions.answer: Top-down expands S to words; bottom-up combines words into S.

knowledgeCheck.question: One sentence can have several parse trees.
'Old men and women' two parses. Reason?

ai-c6-t02.quickRevision: Parsing: grammar+lexicon → parse tree; top-down/bottom-up; CYK O(n³); ambiguity = many trees.
algorithmSteps: Top-down: 1. Start with S.
2. Expand using grammar rules.
3. Match terminals with input words.
4. Backtrack if mismatch; success when all words consumed.
ai-c6-t02.workedExample: S→NP VP, NP→Det N, VP→V NP: 'The cat chased a mouse' ⇒ [S [NP The cat][VP chased [NP a mouse]]].

ai-c6-t03.title: Semantic Analysis
ai-c6-t03.definition: Semantic analysis assigns meaning to syntactic structures, producing a representation of what the sentence says.
ai-c6-t03.simpleExplanation: Syntax ke baad semantic analysis sentence ka matlab nikalta hai: kaun kya kar raha hai, kis par. Word sense disambiguation bhi isi ka hissa hai.
ai-c6-t03.realLifeAnalogy: After checking grammar, you read the sentence to understand who did what to whom.
ai-c6-t03.example: 'Ram ate an apple' → ate(agent=Ram, object=apple) or ∃x apple(x)∧ate(Ram,x).
keyPoints: Maps parse trees to meaning representations (logic forms, frames).
Lexical semantics: word meanings; word-sense disambiguation (bank).
Compositional semantics: meaning of a sentence from its parts.
Approaches: semantic grammars, case grammar, conceptual dependency.
Handles thematic roles: agent, object, instrument.
Ambiguity: lexical and scope.
ifYouKnow: Convert a sentence to a logical form.
commonMistakes: Assuming syntactic correctness implies meaning.
Ignoring multiple word senses.

ai-c6-t04.title: Discourse and Pragmatic Processing
ai-c6-t04.definition: Discourse processing relates sentences across a text (e.g. resolving pronouns), while pragmatic processing interprets language in terms of context, intent and use.
ai-c6-t04.simpleExplanation: Discourse: pichle sentence se connection samajhna (he/she/it kaun hai). Pragmatics: speaker ka asli irada samajhna, jaise 'Can you pass the salt?' ek request hai, sawal nahi.
ai-c6-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Reading a conversation: you remember who 'she' is and understand polite requests hidden inside questions.
ai-c6-t04.example: 'Ravi met Amit. He gave him a book.' Anaphora resolution decides who 'he' and 'him' refer to. 'Can you open the window?' is pragmatically a request.
keyPoints: Discourse: anaphora/coreference resolution, ellipsis, coherence relations.
Pragmatics: speech acts, intention, implicature, world knowledge.
Anaphora types: pronoun, definite noun phrase.
Resolution uses recency, gender/number agreement, salience.
Needs world/context knowledge.
Essential for dialogue systems.
commonMistakes: Using only grammar to resolve pronouns.
Taking indirect requests literally.

ai-c6-t05.title: Spell Checking
ai-c6-t05.definition: Spell checking detects misspelled words and suggests corrections using dictionaries, edit distance and language models.
ai-c6-t05.simpleExplanation: Spell checker pehle galat word pakadta hai (dictionary me nahi hai), phir sabse nazdeeki correct words suggest karta hai (edit distance se).
ai-c6-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A teacher marking a spelling test and writing the closest correct word beside each mistake.
ai-c6-t05.example: 'teh' → candidates 'the' (transposition, distance 1), 'ten', 'tea'. Pick the most frequent/likely: 'the'. Levenshtein(kitten, sitting)=3.
keyPoints: Non-word errors: not in dictionary; real-word errors: valid word in wrong context (their/there).
Detection: dictionary lookup, n-gram models.
Correction: generate candidates within edit distance 1–2, rank by frequency/context.
Edit operations: insert, delete, substitute (Damerau adds transposition).
Levenshtein distance via dynamic programming O(mn).
Soundex/phonetic matching for sound-alike words.
commonMistakes: Thinking dictionary lookup finds real-word errors.
Forgetting transposition as a common typo.

examQuestions.question: Levenshtein distance between 'kitten' and 'sitting'.
examQuestions.answer: 3 (k→s, e→i, insert g).

examQuestions.question: Explain how spell checkers work.
examQuestions.answer: Detect via dictionary/n-grams; generate candidates by edit distance; rank.

knowledgeCheck.question: Non-word vs real-word error.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Non-word is not in the dictionary; real-word is a valid word used wrongly.

ai-c6-t05.quickRevision: Spell check: detect (dictionary/n-gram), correct (edit distance ≤2, rank); real-word errors need context.
algorithmSteps: 1. Tokenise text; look up each word.
2. If not found → generate candidates within edit distance 1–2.
3. Rank candidates by word frequency/context.
4. Suggest top candidates.
ai-c6-t05.complexity: Edit distance DP: O(m·n) time and space for strings of length m and n.

ai-c7-t01.title: Introduction to Neural Networks
ai-c7-t01.definition: An artificial neural network is a computing model of interconnected neurons that compute weighted sums of inputs and pass them through an activation function, learning by adjusting weights.
ai-c7-t01.simpleExplanation: ANN insaani dimaag ke neurons se inspire hai. Har neuron inputs ko weights se multiply karke jodta hai aur activation function se output deta hai. Seekhna matlab weights adjust karna.
ai-c7-t01.realLifeAnalogy: A committee voting: each member (input) has a different influence (weight); the chairman (activation) decides yes/no based on total weighted votes.
ai-c7-t01.example: Neuron: y = f(w1x1 + w2x2 + b). For AND gate with w=(1,1), b=−1.5 and step activation: (1,1)→0.5>0→1; (1,0)→−0.5→0.
keyPoints: Components: inputs, weights, bias, summation, activation function, output.
Activations: step, sigmoid, tanh, ReLU.
Learning = updating weights from data.
McCulloch–Pitts (1943) first model; perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958).
Parallel, distributed, fault tolerant, learns from examples.
Biological neuron: dendrites, soma, axon, synapse.
commonMistakes: Thinking ANN works exactly like the brain.
Forgetting bias.

examQuestions.question: Explain the artificial neuron model.
examQuestions.answer: Inputs, weights, bias, sum, activation, output; analogy with biological neuron.

ai-c7-t01.quickRevision: ANN: y=f(Σwᵢxᵢ+b); learning adjusts weights; activations step/sigmoid/tanh/ReLU.

ai-c7-t02.title: Perception-Qualitative Analysis
ai-c7-t02.definition: Qualitative analysis of the perceptron examines what a single-layer perceptron can and cannot represent, notably linearly separable versus non-separable problems.
ai-c7-t02.simpleExplanation: Syllabus me 'perception-qualitative analysis' likha hai; yahan ise perceptron ka qualitative analysis maana gaya hai: ye kya seekh sakta hai (AND, OR) aur kya nahi (XOR). [Syllabus wording flagged for review.]
ai-c7-t02.realLifeAnalogy: A perceptron is like drawing one straight line to separate red and blue dots: possible only if one line is enough.
ai-c7-t02.example: AND is linearly separable (one line splits (1,1) from the others). XOR is not: (0,1),(1,0) vs (0,0),(1,1) cannot be split by a single line. Update rule: w ← w + η(t−y)x. Start w=(0,0), b=0, input (1,1), target 1, output 0 ⇒ w=(1,1), b=1.
keyPoints: Perceptron: output=step(w·x+b).
Learning rule: w←w+η(t−y)x.
Converges if data is linearly separable (perceptron convergence theorem).
Cannot solve XOR (Minsky & Papert 1969).
Multi-layer networks overcome the limitation.
Qualitative view: capability, limits, convergence, role of η.
commonMistakes: Thinking a perceptron can learn any function.
Confusing 'perception' (sensing) with 'perceptron' (the model).

examQuestions.question: Explain limitations of the perceptron.
examQuestions.answer: Only linearly separable functions; XOR fails; fix with hidden layers.

examQuestions.question: One perceptron update: w=(0,0), b=0, η=1, x=(1,1), t=1, y=0.

knowledgeCheck.question: The perceptron converges for linearly separable data.

ai-c7-t02.quickRevision: Perceptron: w←w+η(t−y)x; learns only linearly separable functions; XOR needs hidden layers.
algorithmSteps: 1. Initialise weights and bias.
2. For each sample compute y=step(w·x+b).
3. Update w←w+η(t−y)x, b←b+η(t−y).
4. Repeat until no errors (or max epochs).
ai-c7-t02.workedExample: AND with η=1: sample (1,1), t=1, y=0 ⇒ error 1 ⇒ w=(1,1), b=1; continue until all four samples classified correctly.

ai-c7-t03.title: Neural Net Architecture and Applications
ai-c7-t03.definition: Neural network architecture is the arrangement of neurons into layers and connections (feed-forward, recurrent, convolutional) that decides what problems the network can solve.
ai-c7-t03.simpleExplanation: Network ka architecture batata hai neurons kitne layers me hain aur kaise jude hain. Feed-forward me signal aage jaata hai; recurrent me loops hote hain; CNN images ke liye hota hai.
ai-c7-t03.realLifeAnalogy: A factory assembly line (feed-forward) vs a team that keeps notes of previous steps (recurrent).
ai-c7-t03.example: XOR with a 2-2-1 feed-forward network: 2 inputs, 2 hidden neurons, 1 output. Hidden neurons learn OR and AND-like features, the output combines them. Trained by backpropagation.
keyPoints: Layers: input, hidden, output.
Single-layer vs multi-layer feed-forward networks.
Recurrent networks have feedback loops (sequence data).
CNNs for images; RNN/LSTM for sequences.
Backpropagation: forward pass, error, backward gradient, weight update.
Applications: image/speech recognition, forecasting, medical diagnosis, NLP, control.
commonMistakes: Thinking more layers always means better accuracy.
Confusing recurrent with feed-forward.

ai-c7-t04.title: Utilization and Functionality
ai-c7-t04.definition: Utilization and functionality describe how neural networks are used in practice (training, validation, deployment) and the tasks they perform, such as classification, regression, clustering and association.
ai-c7-t04.simpleExplanation: Neural network ko use karne ke steps: data taiyaar karo, train karo, validate karo, deploy karo. Wo classification, prediction, clustering jaise kaam karta hai.
ai-c7-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Training a new employee: teach with examples, test on unseen cases, then assign real work.
ai-c7-t04.example: Spam classifier: collect labelled emails → split train/validation/test → train → check accuracy and overfitting → deploy to the mail server.
keyPoints: Learning types: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement.
Functions: classification, regression, pattern association, clustering, function approximation.
Workflow: data → preprocess → train → validate → test → deploy.
Overfitting: good on training data, poor on new data; fix via more data, regularisation, early stopping.
Strengths: learns complex patterns, noise tolerant.
Limits: needs data, black box, compute heavy.
commonMistakes: Testing on training data only.
Treating NN as an always-explainable model.

ai-c7-t05.title: Architecture of the Expert System
ai-c7-t05.definition: An expert system is a program that emulates a human expert's decision making using a knowledge base and an inference engine.
ai-c7-t05.simpleExplanation: Expert system ek software hai jo kisi expert (doctor, engineer) ki tarah decision leta hai. Isme knowledge base, inference engine, user interface, explanation facility aur knowledge acquisition hote hain.
ai-c7-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A call-centre agent with a thick rulebook (knowledge base), a way of choosing the right rule (inference engine) and a screen to talk to the caller (user interface).
ai-c7-t05.example: Medical diagnosis ES: knowledge base has rules about symptoms; the user enters symptoms; the inference engine chains rules; the explanation facility says 'Diagnosis X because fever AND rash'.
keyPoints: Knowledge base: facts and rules from the expert.
Inference engine: forward/backward chaining to reason.
Working memory: current case facts.
User interface: communicates with the user.
Explanation facility: shows how/why a conclusion was reached.
Knowledge acquisition module: updates the knowledge base; people: domain expert, knowledge engineer, user.
commonMistakes: Mixing knowledge base with database.
Forgetting the explanation facility.

examQuestions.answer: Draw: user interface ↔ inference engine ↔ knowledge base; working memory; explanation; acquisition.

examQuestions.question: Expert system vs conventional program.
examQuestions.answer: ES separates knowledge from control, can explain, uses heuristics; conventional programs mix logic and data.

ai-c7-t06.title: Knowledge Representation in Expert Systems
ai-c7-t06.definition: Expert systems represent knowledge mainly as production rules, supplemented by frames, semantic networks, logic and certainty factors.
ai-c7-t06.simpleExplanation: Expert system me knowledge zyada tar IF-THEN rules me hota hai. Kabhi frames ya semantic nets bhi, aur uncertainty ke liye certainty factors.
ai-c7-t06.realLifeAnalogy: A doctor's notebook of 'if this symptom then that' tips, each tagged with how sure she is.
ai-c7-t06.example: Rule: IF fever=yes AND rash=yes THEN disease=measles (CF=0.7). Frame: Patient{age, symptoms, history}.
keyPoints: Production rules (IF–THEN) are most common.
Frames hold structured objects/defaults.
Semantic nets, logic can complement.
Certainty factors attach uncertainty to rules.
Knowledge acquisition bottleneck: extracting expert knowledge is slow.
Rule-based knowledge is modular and explainable.
commonMistakes: Thinking rules can capture all expert intuition.
Ignoring rule conflicts.

ai-c7-t07.title: Two Case Studies on Expert Systems
ai-c7-t07.definition: Case studies such as MYCIN (medical diagnosis) and DENDRAL (chemical structure elucidation) show how expert systems encode expert knowledge to solve real problems.
ai-c7-t07.simpleExplanation: Do mashhoor expert systems: MYCIN (bacterial infection diagnosis, antibiotics suggest) aur DENDRAL (molecule ka structure nikalna). [Syllabus ne names nahi diye; ye do chune gaye hain — apne notes se confirm karo.]
ai-c7-t07.realLifeAnalogy: MYCIN is a medical specialist in a box; DENDRAL is a chemist who reads a mass-spectrometer graph and proposes the molecule.
ai-c7-t07.example: MYCIN: input symptoms and lab results; ~600 IF–THEN rules with certainty factors; backward chaining; output likely organism and suggested antibiotic with explanations. DENDRAL: input mass-spectrometry data; plan–generate–test; output candidate molecular structures.
keyPoints: MYCIN (Stanford, 1970s): diagnoses blood infections; rule-based; backward chaining; certainty factors; explanation facility; never used in routine clinical practice.
DENDRAL (Stanford, 1960s–70s): infers molecular structure from mass spectrometry; plan–generate–test; first successful expert system.
XCON/R1 (DEC) configured VAX computers using forward chaining (additional example).
Lessons: rules + explanation + domain restriction work well.
Limits: brittle, narrow domain, knowledge acquisition effort.
Influenced modern clinical decision support.
commonMistakes: Saying MYCIN was deployed in hospitals (it was a research system).
Mixing up MYCIN (medicine) and DENDRAL (chemistry).
